column3: [AI Project] Scout — Page/DOM Awareness for AI Assistant
column5:
Currently Scout has no awareness of what page the user is on or what content is displayed on that page. This was identified as the top priority gap during the June 16, 2026 AI sync (Ron + Sadaf) and confirmed by Sadaf as not yet implemented or scoped.

Context: Ron's goal is for Scout to know which page a user is on and what's visible on it, so users can interact with on-page content directly through Scout without copy/pasting — e.g. "Scout, change the reading level of the article I'm looking at" or "where is X on this page." This is considered the main blocker preventing Scout from being released to internal stakeholders for feedback.

Next step: dedicated planning meeting scheduled for Wednesday, June 24, 2026 between Ron and Sadaf to define requirements before implementation begins.

Related: ONLINE-6806 (chat modal persistence/movability) is a separate but adjacent improvement — this ticket covers DOM/content awareness specifically, not modal positioning.

h3. +Key Topics+

h4. +1.+ +*Navigating the Classrooms Page*+

The Classrooms page is where teachers can manage their classrooms, including finding, creating, archiving, and viewing classrooms. Key actions include:


* *Refresh Button*: Refresh the list of classrooms.
* *Active/Inactive*: Swap between active and inactive classrooms.
* *Search*: Type the name of a classroom you have access to.
* *Create Classroom*: Follow steps to create a new classroom if your district is not using a single sign-on.
* *Classroom Expiration*: Notification will appear 30 days prior to expiration for manually created classrooms.

[Studies Weekly Help Center: How to Navigate the Classrooms Page|https://support.studiesweekly.com/hc/en-us/articles/5343280936475-How-to-Navigate-the-Classrooms-Page]


h4. +2.+ +*Navigating the People Page*+

The People page allows teachers to manage other teacher and student accounts that have access to the classroom. Key actions include:


* *Invite Teacher to the Classroom*: Add a co-teacher to your classroom.
* *Bulk Actions*: Add Coins or Remove teachers in bulk.
* *Find Teacher*: Search for an assigned teacher in the current classroom.
* *Sort by*: Sort the teacher list by first name, last name, or username.
* *Teacher Actions*: Add Coins or Remove individual teachers from accessing the classroom.

13/Jul/26 12:41 PM;557058:e2772c51-ac82-4560-9ea8-4a11a9315d77;Adding some general guidelines here so we can apply this to every page, not just account settings.

Every page Scout knows about should be able to answer "what is this page / what can I do here" the same way:

# Identify the page in one line using its human name. "You're on the article Title" or "This is your account settings page." No internal IDs or raw data ever show up in a response.
# Tell the user what they can do here. 2 to 4 things, phrased as actions, based on what is actually on the page and who the user is.
# End with a next step. "What would you like to do?" or offer to walk them through something. Keep it short.

If Scout can't see or answer something from the current page, it should just say so and point to where it lives. "I can't see that from this page, you can find grades under X." It should never guess.

Examples:

Article page: "You're on the article [Article Title] from [Week/Unit]. I can summarize it, explain any part of it, read it with you, or answer questions about it. What would you like to do?"

Account settings: "This is your account settings page. You can update your profile info like name, email, and password here. Want me to walk you through changing something?"

"where am I" on any page: "You're on [page name] in [publication/section]. Want a quick rundown of what you can do here?"

"help" on any page: short list of what Scout can do on the current page plus 2 or 3 example questions the user could ask.

The bar for testing: every page in Scout's catalog can produce a response that follows 1 through 3. If a page can't, that's a gap we need to fill, not a reason for a generic fallback answer.

Students will be able to identify the three levels of government (federal, state, local) and name the leader at each level (president, governor, mayor).

Students will be able to describe at least one responsibility of each level of government using information from the text.

Sticky notes

## Key vocabulary

Note: the retrieved excerpt of the article text did not fully show definitions in context; use these terms as they appear in the lesson plans and vocabulary list, and confirm exact in-text definitions when you read the article with students.

**civic responsibility** — a duty citizens share as part of a community (confirm definition in text)

**separation of powers** — dividing government roles among different parts (confirm definition in text)

**common good** — what benefits the community as a whole (confirm definition in text)

**federal, state, local** — the three levels of government named in the article

**branches of government** — the three parts of government at each level, shown in the article's image

## Warm-up (about a tenth of the period)

Create a class KWL chart with three columns: K (know), W (want to know), L (learned).

Ask students to think independently and write down what they know about our government on a piece of paper.

Ask students to share what they wrote with a partner.

As a class, share out and build a common list in the "K" column.

Ask students to write questions they have about government; record these in the "W" column (or have students post individual sticky notes so they can be moved to "L" later).

**Keep this KWL chart posted — it will be used across the week's lessons.**

## Reading (about a quarter of the period)

Students read "The United States Government" independently or as a class (teacher's choice based on reading levels).

**Stop-and-think questions:**

After the paragraph introducing levels of government: "What are the three levels of government named here? Why do you think a country might need more than one level of government?"

After the paragraph(s) describing responsibilities: "What is one responsibility you just read about? Which level of government handles it?"

Before finishing: "What words in this section are new to you or confusing?"

**During reading, have students:**

Circle the different levels of government (federal, state, local).

Underline the responsibilities at each level of government.

After reading, ask students what words they have questions about, and help define those as a class (answers will vary).

## Discussion (about a fifth of the period)

**(Recall)** What are the three levels of government? *Look for: federal, state, local.*

**(Recall)** Who is the leader at the city level? At the state level? Of the nation? *Look for: mayor, governor, president.*

**(Comprehension)** What is one responsibility you underlined for each level? *Look for: specific examples pulled from the text, correctly matched to the right level.*

**(Reasoning)** Why do you think government responsibilities are divided among different levels instead of handled by just one group? *Look for: reasoning that different levels may handle different-sized problems or areas — accept any reasonable, text-supported idea; this is not stated directly in the article, so treat student answers as inference, not fact.*

**(Reasoning)** Looking at the image in "Three Branches of Government," why do you think government is also divided into three branches at each level? *Look for: student inference — encourage them to connect it to the previous question about dividing responsibility.*

## Activity (about a third of the period)

**Part A — Elected Leaders (individual/partner):**

Watch the video "Public Officials," asking students to watch for the leaders at the city, state, and national level.

Distribute the "Our Elected Leaders" graphic organizer.

Have students work with a partner to complete it, recording the leader and role at each level.

**Part B — Three Branches jigsaw (small groups):**

Explain that each level of government also has three branches.

Ask students to look at the image in "Three Branches of Government" and circle the names of the three branches they find.

As a class, read the first paragraph together.

Divide the class into three groups; assign each group one branch of government.

Each group reads independently about their assigned branch and completes that section of the "Branches of the United States Government" graphic organizer.

Within groups, students share with two or three others what they recorded as a responsibility for their branch.

Each group reports out to the whole class; all students complete the remaining sections of their graphic organizer as other groups share.

**Product:** A completed "Our Elected Leaders" organizer and a completed "Branches of the United States Government" organizer per student.

**Close:** Return to the KWL chart and record what students learned in the "L" column, moving or answering questions from the "W" column.

## Differentiation

**English learners:** Pre-teach the words "level," "branch," and "responsibility" before reading; pair with a supportive partner during the graphic organizer tasks; allow pointing to text or images when sharing out.

**Struggling readers:** Read the article aloud as a class rather than independently; provide the completed circle/underline steps as a model on the board first; allow oral responses for the graphic organizers with a partner or scribe.

**Advanced students:** Ask them to compare a responsibility from one branch to a responsibility from another branch and explain, in writing, why they think each is assigned to a different branch (frame as their own reasoning, since the article does not state a reason).

Name the three levels of government.

Who is the leader at the state level?

Name one of the three branches of government and one responsibility you learned about for that branch.

**Answer key:**

Federal, state, local.

Governor.

Answers will vary based on the branch each student's group researched; accept any branch name paired with a responsibility recorded on that group's graphic organizer.

Arizona Studies Weekly – Past and Present: Full Publication Overview

# Arizona Studies Weekly – Past and Present: Full Publication Overview

## Overview

**Grade:** Not stated on this page — inferred as upper elementary (grade 3–4) from unit and week topics (Civics, Geography, Economics, Inquiry, History and Culture).

**Subject:** Social Studies (Arizona Studies Weekly)

**Time:** One class period

**Summary:** Students preview the whole year of "Past and Present" by exploring its five units and 32 weeks, so they understand how the course is organized before diving into individual weeks.

**Timing:** adjust to your period length.

## Learning objectives (Scout's draft)

Students will be able to name the 5 units of the publication and give the topic of each.

Students will be able to locate a given week's title within its correct unit using the table of contents.

Students will be able to sequence the weeks within Unit 5: History and Culture in the order they appear (Life in the Americas through A Year in Review).

Students will be able to generate at least one question they want answered by a specific week's content.

## Materials

The table of contents (units and weeks) for "Arizona Studies Weekly – Past and Present"

Student copies or a projected version of the unit/week list

Chart paper or whiteboard divided into 5 columns (one per unit)

Sticky notes (one set per student or pair)

## Key vocabulary

**Civics and Government** — the unit about government, important documents, rights, and citizens.

**Geography** — the unit about themes of geography like place, movement, and human-environment interaction.

**Economics** — the unit about needs, wants, resources, and economic systems.

**Inquiry** — the unit about asking questions, finding sources, and drawing conclusions.

**History and Culture** — the unit about life in the Americas, exploration, colonies, and conflicts like the French and Indian War.

## Warm-up (about a tenth of the period)

Ask students: "This year we will study 5 big units with 32 weeks of topics. Just from the unit names — Civics and Government, Geography, Economics, Inquiry, History and Culture — what do you think each one might be about?" Take quick verbal guesses for each unit name, no wrong answers, to activate prior knowledge before revealing the real week titles.

## Reading (about a quarter of the period)

Display the table of contents. Read through it unit by unit, pausing at three points:

**After Unit 1 (Civics and Government, Weeks 1–5):** Stop-and-think — "Which of these five week titles (Government, Important Documents, The Bill of Rights, Citizens, Founders) do you think comes first, and why might it come first?"

**After Unit 4 (Inquiry, Weeks 16–21):** Stop-and-think — "Notice the week titles: Historical Inquiry, Developing Inquiries, Sources, Analyzing and Evaluating Evidence, Communicating Conclusions, Engaging in Your Own Inquiry. What steps do you think this unit is teaching, in order?"

**After Unit 5 (History and Culture, Weeks 22–32):** Stop-and-think — "This unit ends with 'A Year in Review.' Why do you think that title comes last?"

## Discussion (about a fifth of the period)

**Recall:** How many units are in this publication? How many weeks total? (5 units; 32 weeks.)

**Recall:** Which unit has the most weeks, and which has the fewest? (Unit 5: History and Culture has 11 weeks; Unit 3: Economics has 4 weeks.)

**Reasoning:** Unit 5 includes weeks titled Jamestown, Plymouth, Colonial Life, Clash of the Empires, and Consequences of the French and Indian War. Why do you think these are grouped under "History and Culture" rather than under "Geography" or "Economics"?

**Reasoning:** Unit 4 is called "Inquiry" and includes weeks like Sources and Analyzing and Evaluating Evidence. Why might a social studies course teach students how to investigate before teaching all the history?

**Reasoning:** Look at Unit 2 (Geography): Five Themes of Geography, Map Skills, Place, Human-Environment Interaction, Movement, Culture. Why do you think "Five Themes of Geography" comes first in that unit?

**Look-fors:** Students correctly identify unit and week counts from the table of contents; students give a reasonable (not necessarily "correct") justification tied to the actual titles, not outside knowledge; students recognize sequencing patterns (skills before content, general before specific).

## Activity (about a third of the period)

**"Map the Year" — Unit Sorting and Question-Writing**

**Grouping:** Pairs or small groups (one group per unit works well with 5 groups, or all groups do all 5 units in a rotation).

**Steps:**

Give each pair the list of week titles for one unit (or the full list if doing all five).

Groups write their assigned unit's week titles, in the correct order, onto sticky notes — one week title per note.

Groups place their sticky notes in order on the matching column of the class chart (labeled with the 5 unit names).

For each unit, the group writes one question on a separate sticky note that they hope the unit will answer (e.g., for Unit 5: "Why did colonists and other groups clash during the French and Indian War?").

Groups post their question sticky note under their unit column.

Whole class does a quick walk-by "gallery view" of all 5 completed columns.

**Product:** A class-built visual map of all 5 units and their weeks in order, plus one guiding question per unit, displayed in the room for the rest of the year.

## Differentiation

**English learners:** Provide the unit and week titles pre-printed on cards to reduce copying; allow question-writing in home language first, then translate together as a pair.

**Struggling readers:** Pair with a stronger reader; reduce the task to ordering only 3–4 week titles instead of a full unit; use unit names as anchor words already written on the chart.

**Advanced students:** Ask them to sort all 5 units (not just one), or to predict how Unit 4 (Inquiry) skills might be used later in Unit 5 (History and Culture) topics.

## Assessment / exit ticket (about a tenth of the period)

Name the 5 units in this publication.

Which unit contains the week titled "Jamestown"?

List the weeks of Unit 3: Economics in order.

**Answer key:**

Civics and Government; Geography; Economics; Inquiry; History and Culture.

Unit 5: History and Culture.

Needs and Wants; Resources; Economic Principles; Economic Systems.

{noformat}This one is in noticeably better shape than the Government lesson plan — the numbers actually cross-check correctly, and the hedge-language problem from before doesn't show up here. A few things worth noting either way:

What checks out well:

The unit/week math is internally consistent. Working backward from the ranges given (Unit 1: weeks 1–5, Unit 4: weeks 16–21, Unit 5: weeks 22–32) and the stated counts (Unit 3 = 4 weeks, Unit 5 = 11 weeks), Unit 2 works out to weeks 6–11 (6 weeks) and Unit 3 to weeks 12–15 (4 weeks). That gives 5+6+4+6+11 = 32, which matches the "32 weeks" stated in the summary — and it also matches the actual count of week titles listed for each unit (5 titles for Unit 1, 6 for Unit 2, 4 for Unit 3, 6 for Unit 4). Everything lines up.

The Overview fields (Grade/Subject/Time/Summary) are each on their own line this time, unlike the previous lesson plan where they were merged into one run-on paragraph. Good sign that the earlier formatting issue may have been a one-off rather than systemic — worth keeping an eye on whether it recurs elsewhere.

No leaked hedge/caveat language this time (no "confirm in text," no "treat as inference, not fact"). That suggests the earlier issue may have been specific to that article's incomplete excerpt rather than a general generation problem.

Objectives map cleanly onto the assessment questions (name the 5 units → Q1, Jamestown's unit → Q2 and matches the Unit 5 list from the Discussion section, Unit 3 week order → Q3 and matches the count established earlier).

Worth flagging:

No Standards section at all. The Government lesson plan at least had an explicit "Standards aren't linked for this page" line disclosing the gap. This plan omits Standards entirely — no section, no disclosure. If Standards is supposed to be a required section across all lesson plans, its complete absence here (rather than an explicit "not available" note) is arguably worse than the previous case, since there's no way to tell if it was skipped intentionally or dropped by a bug.

Timing percentages don't sum to 100% — same pattern as the previous lesson plan: 10% + 25% + 20% + 33% + 10% = 98%. Since this is the second lesson plan in a row with the same ~98% total, it's worth checking whether this is a systemic issue with how the period-breakdown template rounds, rather than a one-off.

"Grade 3–4" should probably read "Grades 3–4" (plural) — minor grammar nit, not functional.

Unit 5's exact week sequence (Objective 3 asks students to sequence "Life in the Americas through A Year in Review") can't be verified against the real table of contents from here — worth a quick manual check that the actual TOC order matches what's implied, since I don't have the source document to cross-reference.{noformat}

column3: [AI Project] AI Text Leveler Training
column5:
We need to train out AI Text Leveler to the different grade levels of text based on our Publications and the Grade levels they are associated with.  

h3. Summary

We need to train our AI Text Leveler to adjust text for different grade levels.

h3. Context

This training is based on our Publications and the specific grade levels they are associated with.

h3. Requirements

* AI Text Leveler must be able to adjust text 2 grades above and below the text. (2-8).
**  For 1, it can only go down to K.
** K, can only go up by 2 levels
* Training should utilize existing SW Publications as a reference for text of each grade level.
* How does SW Lexile? from our Curriculum team.
** When I think about Lexile, I don’t think of it as dumbing content down. I think of it as managing how much work a student has to do to understand what they’re reading. Most of the time, Lexile comes down to how ideas are presented, not what ideas are included.
From an editing standpoint, these are the main things I pay attention to, and the things I actually change when I need to move a text up or down:
*Sentence structure and length*
This is usually the biggest lever for me.
*** Shorter, cleaner sentences almost always bring the Lexile down.
*** Long sentences with multiple clauses, stacked ideas, or passive phrasing push it up.
*** Splitting one long sentence into two or three clear ones can make a big difference without changing the meaning at all.
** *Vocabulary*
Vocabulary matters, but it’s tricky.
*** Common, concrete words generally lower Lexile.
*** Abstract or academic wording raises it.
*** I’ll swap out unnecessarily complex words when a clearer option works just as well.
** That said, this is where automation can get complicated. Often, the vocabulary we use has to be very specific. It may be tied directly to a standard, required by a particular state, or essential to the content being taught. In those cases, we cannot simply replace a word with an easier synonym without changing what students are expected to learn.
Because of that, it could be helpful if a tool either allowed for, or worked alongside, a way to input required standards, key terms, or word preferences for a project. That way, the algorithm could respect vocabulary that must stay while still helping with sentence structure and clarity elsewhere.
*Idea density*
I’m always watching how much is packed into each sentence.
*** I aim for one main idea per sentence.
*** If a sentence is explaining cause, effect, and an example all at once, I’ll usually break that apart.
*** Headings and paragraph breaks don’t change the Lexile score directly, but they help me see where the text feels overloaded.
** *Grammar and phrasing choices*
Certain constructions consistently push Lexile up:
*** Passive voice
*** Turning verbs into nouns, like “the expansion of” instead of “expanded”
*** Conditional or hypothetical phrasing
** I don’t avoid these completely, but I try to use them intentionally rather than by habit.
*Clarity and repetition*
*** Repeating key terms, instead of constantly switching to pronouns or synonyms, often helps both clarity and Lexile.
*** Being specific about who or what a sentence is referring to usually makes the sentence simpler and easier to process.
*** When something is clearer, the Lexile almost always improves.
** *What I don’t do*
*** I don’t cut essential content just to hit a number.
*** I don’t oversimplify ideas in a way that changes meaning.
*** I don’t rely only on swapping words. Structure matters more.
** *Big-picture thought for an algorithm*
From an editor’s perspective, a really helpful leveling tool would pay close attention to sentence length, clause complexity, and how many ideas are packed into a sentence, not just vocabulary. Most of the work we do to adjust Lexile is about reshaping how ideas are delivered while still honoring required language and standards.
If I had to summarize my approach, when I’m trying to hit a target Lexile, I start with sentence structure, then idea load, and then word choice, within the constraints of the standards we are working toward.
** one specific trick to lower the lexile–removing gerund endings (“worked” instead of “was working”).
** In lowering Lexile levels simplifying sentences and removing unnecessary descriptors/modifiers (adjectives, prepositional phrases, etc.) is a good place to start. But as stated above, we have to be careful, because sometimes that text is tied into standards or key concepts for understanding. One thing I’ve learned about Lexile is there aren’t very many fast, firm rules: Every time I think I’ve found “the answer,” I find as many exceptions as successes. So whatever programming we try to implement, we’ll want to make sure that it’s thoroughly tested and reviewed and, even after that, perhaps have a human review the changes to ensure that key information isn’t removed. I’m probably just stating the obvious.

column3: [AI Project] Model comparison report — accuracy/cost tradeoffs for Scout (Nova Micro vs. larger models)
column5:
During the June 16, 2026 AI sync, Sadaf offered to produce a report comparing response accuracy and reliability across AI model tiers available in AWS Bedrock (e.g. Nova Micro, the current cheapest/smallest model, vs. Nova Lite/Pro/Premier or other mid/large tiers), alongside the cost difference for each.

Purpose: Ron needs concrete numbers (estimated success/failure rates and relative cost multipliers) to bring to the executive team when discussing the AI product's quality-vs-cost tradeoffs and pricing strategy.

Context: current Nova Micro performance was informally estimated by Sadaf at roughly 70% success rate for following response format and avoiding wrong URLs. Moving to Nova Premier was roughly estimated as 3-4x the cost. A more rigorous side-by-side comparison would help quantify this properly.

Deliverable: a short report or writeup showing model options, estimated accuracy/success rate per model, and relative cost, to support stakeholder conversations.

column7:
10/Sep/26 6:48 AM;62850ed5bdf2f30067d3f477;This comparison has been done. Summary below; the full working is in {{docs/AiAssistantModelEvaluation.md}}, and the instruments are kept in {{rag/experiments/model_eval/}} for re-running.

*Method:* real Bedrock calls (not estimates), measured per feature rather than only on routing, across Nova Micro, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, with gpt-oss-120b added for question generation. Completed 2026-08-24.

----

h2. Headline: two of the ticket's starting numbers need correcting

# *Nova Premier is not 3–4× the cost. It is ~70–90×.*

Bedrock's own published token pricing, relative to Nova Micro:

||Model||Input||Output||
|Nova Micro _(current)_|1×|1×|
|Nova Lite|1.7×|1.7×|
|gpt-oss-120b|4.3×|4.3×|
|Claude Haiku 4.5|7.1×|~10× measured per turn|
|Nova Pro|22.9×|22.9×|
|Nova Premier|*71×*|*89×*|
|Claude Sonnet 4.5|85.7×|~128× measured per turn|

Measured per-turn cost on our actual traffic shape: Nova Micro *$0.00037*, Haiku *$0.0036*, Sonnet *$0.047*. Latency scales too — 2.3s / 4.7s / 8.1s, with some Sonnet turns hitting 16–23s.

# *The 70% success estimate was pessimistic on routing.* Measured routing accuracy on a 22-ask benchmark: *Nova Micro 90.5%*, Haiku 93.4%, Sonnet 90.3%. Moving to Claude buys *+2.9 points for ~10× the cost*; Sonnet buys nothing at ~128×.

----

h2. The wrong-URL problem is solved, and not by model choice

This is worth stating plainly because it changes what a bigger model would buy us.

We hit invented URLs twice. Both times the model had been explicitly instructed not to invent one — removing the first bad pattern simply moved the invention to a second shape. *Prompting did not fix it; a code-level rule did:* a link now survives into a reply only if it appeared in a tool result on that same turn. It is enforced in the codebase and covered by tests.

A more expensive model would not have fixed this, and does not now protect against it. *This class of error is an engineering problem, and it is closed.*

----

h2. What we found per feature — no model is uniformly better

The first pass suggested a clean Nova win. Closing the remaining criteria changed that picture, and surfaced real defects *on both sides*:

||Dimension||Result||
|Question generation — mechanical quality|*Wash.* 14–15/15 usable across all four models|
|Question generation — plural requests|*Nova wins decisively.* "Make me some questions" → Nova generates 3/3; both Claude models ask a clarifying question 0/3 instead|
|Question generation — grounding|*Sonnet loses.* 2/3 runs handed back a verbatim on-page question as "new" — the most expensive model failed hardest on the thing we most need to trust|
|Article adaptation — content retention|*Wash.* 85–125% retained on real 1,000+ word articles|
|Article adaptation — reading level|*Claude wins.* Nova barely moves some articles (grade 8.6 → 8.2 on a "rewrite for grade 2" request)|
|Article adaptation — ambiguous requests|*Claude wins.* Nova acted without confirming on 1/3 ambiguous asks; both Claude models asked every time|
|Support answers|*No consistent winner.* Each model was clearly better on one real question and clearly worse on another|
|Action execution ({{verify()}})|*Wash.* Nova 5/5, Haiku 5/5 — actions genuinely completed, confirmed in a real browser|

The pattern: *Nova is more decisive and occasionally wrong; Claude is more cautious and asks more.* Neither is safe everywhere. Nova's failures are an under-simplified article or an occasionally wrong support answer. Claude's are a clarifying question where a teacher wanted an answer.

----

h2. Where we landed — and it isn't one model

We did not pick a single model. *We picked per purpose*, which is the part I'd emphasise for the exec conversation:

* *Conversation and routing → Nova Micro.* Nothing tested justified 10× for +2.9 points, and Sonnet's grounding failure disqualifies it outright for content teachers are meant to trust.
* *Question generation → moved off Nova Micro to gpt-oss-120b* (4.3× Nova's price, still ~20× cheaper than Sonnet). Nova Micro could not reliably return a full generated question, and gpt-oss has native structured-output support and a far larger context window. This shipped 2026-08-24, with Nova retained as a one-line rollback.

So the honest position is: *the cheapest model handles the conversation, and we spent money only where the cheap model measurably failed.* That is a deliberate cost/quality split rather than a single-tier bet.

----

h2. What this doesn't cover

Stated so the numbers aren't over-read:

* *Sample sizes are small* — most tables are 3 runs across 1–4 articles or questions. Enough to see a pattern, not enough to rule out run-to-run noise on the closer calls, support answers especially.
* *Nova Lite, Pro and Premier were not behaviourally tested.* The cost figures above are Bedrock's published pricing; the accuracy comparison covered Nova Micro against the Claude tiers. If Ron wants Premier numbers specifically, that is a further run — though at ~70–90× it would need to be dramatically better to change anything.
* *These figures are from 2026-08-24.* Model availability on our account shifts (several model IDs in our config are already dead), so liveness would need re-checking before acting on any switch.

----

h2. Suggested framing for the exec conversation

# *We are already at ~90% on routing*, not 70%, and the specific failure that prompted the concern — invented URLs — has been fixed in code and cannot be fixed by spending more on a model.
# *The next tier up costs ~10× and buys ~3 percentage points*, with trade-offs that are worse in places, not just better.
# *Premier is ~70–90×, not 3–4×* — that number should not go into a pricing discussion uncorrected.
# *We already spend selectively* where the cheap model genuinely failed. The strategy is not "use the cheapest thing everywhere"; it's "use the cheapest thing that measurably works, per feature."

column3: [AI Project] Scout: filter teacher resources by publication, unit, week
column5:
_AI-suggested — not yet validated_

This ticket was suggested by AI (Scout). Before starting work, confirm the issue is real, the proposed fix still makes sense, and it is worth prioritizing.

*Priority:* Sprint · *Repo:* rag

Teachers should be able to ask Scout in chat for specific teacher resources and media and get the right items back as result cards: printables, worksheets, the weekly or unit assessment, rubrics, images, videos and audio. A request can name a publication, unit or week, e.g. "Find the weekly assessment for 4th Grade Social Studies, unit 2, week 3", "Printables for week 5", "Videos for week 3", "Find audio about Martin Luther King Jr."

*Current behaviour* (measured 2026-09-25 on local, 8 real requests, feedback-2026-09-22/results/resource-search-demo.md):

* Type-only requests work: videos 6/6 on topic; no audio about MLK exists, and Scout correctly said so.
* Anything naming a publication, unit or week doesn't: the weekly assessment for publication 68, unit 7, week 16 was never found; printables for American Foundations returned 2 printables out of 6 cards, neither from that publication; videos for week 16 were 3/6 from the right publication, with none confirmed for that week.
* Images and videos come back mixed.

Unit and week are only search words, a publication named in the request isn't applied as a filter, and media items carry no unit or week information.

*Scope (rag only):*

* Publication, unit and week filters in Scout's curriculum search; resolve a named publication and "unit N, week M" to ids.
* Keep image and video results separate when the teacher asks for one.
* During content sync, give media items the unit and week of the articles they belong to.
* Recognise "audio" (and similar wording) as a media type.
* Re-sync content on dev and production.

*Acceptance criteria:*

* A request naming a publication, unit and week returns only items from that week, of the requested type, or says clearly that none exist.
* Media results can be narrowed by week; audio requests return audio.
* Requests without a unit or week behave as today.
* Measured against current behaviour on a fixed set of teacher requests; manual test steps for dev.

*Out of scope:* swo-3.0 export or chat UI changes, unless the investigation shows they're needed (raised before work starts).

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-01: Honest, Evidence-Based Scout
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Foundation

*Objective:* Make today's Scout trustworthy before it does more. Every answer says where Scout looked and why it said what it said, weak matches disappear, and every student-related feature meets one shared bar for evidence and wording before any teacher sees it.

*Problem:* In the audit, "I'm teaching photosynthesis tomorrow" on an account with expired publications returned unrelated social studies vocabulary before admitting nothing matched. A teacher cannot tell what "nothing found" means. Most later tickets say something about children; without shared rules, one careless sentence about a child damages trust in all of them.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks for content and sees only relevant results, with a line saying where Scout searched, and a plain reason when nothing matches.
* Whenever Scout says something about a student or class, the evidence (scores, dates, answers) sits beside it, with a way to open the underlying work.
* The teacher can mark any answer as wrong or not useful.
* Example requests: "Do I have anything on Rosa Parks?", "Why can't I find the lesson on ecosystems?", "Why did you say Dolly is falling behind?", "That's not right, she was absent that week.", "What information about my students do you use?"

*Scope:*

* _Honest, relevant search (former 1.2):_ hide results that only share a keyword with the request; state where Scout looked; the three-way "not found / elsewhere in your publications / not in your school's publications" distinction; works on Scout's current content finding.
* _Trust, evidence and safe wording (former 1.3):_ evidence beside every claim about a student or class; describe what a student did, never what a student is; no labels, diagnoses or predictions about a child; supports framed as suggestions, not judgements; a "wrong / not useful" control on every answer, reviewed by the team; terms such as "behind" or "struggling" recorded as placeholders for the curriculum and content team to confirm; a release checklist every student feature passes (teacher-judged review on real examples, internal and volunteer classrooms first).
* _Already built and kept:_ student names are hidden from the AI and restored only for the teacher.

*Out of scope:*

* Searching every content type across every publication (SCOUT-05).
* Purchase or trial suggestions for publications the school does not own.
* Student-facing AI; formal legal or compliance review.

*Depends on:* None.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# On a set of real teacher content requests agreed before testing, no result appears that only shares a word with the request.
# Every content answer names where Scout looked.
# When content exists only in a publication the teacher's school does not have, Scout says so, does not present it as available and does not suggest buying it.
# When content exists in another of the teacher's own publications, Scout names that publication and offers to open it.
# When nothing relevant exists, Scout says it found nothing and does not pad the answer with unrelated items.
# Every statement about a named student or class is shown with the evidence behind it, and the teacher can open the underlying work.
# A reviewer reading a sample of student-related answers finds no labels, diagnoses or predictions about a child.
# The teacher can mark any answer as wrong or not useful, and the report reaches the team.
# Student names appear only to the teacher who teaches that student.
# The release checklist is written down and applied before any later student feature (SCOUT-04, 06, 10 to 15) is shown to teachers.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Who reviews teacher feedback, and how often, needs an owner.
* The definitions of "behind" and "struggling" wait on the curriculum and content team.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-02: Scout Remembers Teacher Context
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Foundation

*Objective:* Stop Scout asking for things SWO already knows, such as grade, subject, state and publications, and let it remember what the teacher tells it. The teacher can always see what Scout assumed and correct it.

*Problem:* Scout's question form asks for publication, grade and question type every time. Classroom settings already hold grade, subject and dates, but Scout does not use them outside the page on screen. Scout's history shows repeated kinds of request (rubrics, crosswords, lesson plans) that it does not learn from.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks for a quiz and Scout drafts it for the right grade, state and usual format without asking, and says what it assumed ("Grade 4, Michigan standards, your usual 5-question format").
* The teacher states a preference once and Scout applies it in later conversations.
* The teacher opens "What Scout knows about me" and edits or deletes anything.
* Example requests: "Make a quiz on this week's article.", "I teach Grade 4 in Michigan.", "Always give me questions in Spanish too.", "What do you remember about me?", "Forget my format preference."

*Scope:*

* _Known context (former 11.1, 11.3):_ classroom grade, subject, state, dates and publications used from any page, so Scout's understanding of the teacher, class and publication no longer depends on the page open.
* _Remembered preferences (former 11.1, 11.2):_ stated preferences and common kinds of request, reused so the teacher is not asked again.
* _Visible assumptions:_ answers that rely on context say what was assumed, in plain words.
* _Teacher control:_ a clear view where the teacher can see, change and delete what Scout remembers.
* Where classroom details are blank or look like placeholders, Scout asks once and remembers rather than guessing.

*Out of scope:*

* Anything learned about students (SCOUT-04 and SCOUT-10).
* Sharing a teacher's context with other teachers or administrators.
* Turning Teacher Notes or chat history into context.

*Depends on:* None. It improves SCOUT-05, 07, 08 and 09.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# A teacher whose classroom grade and state are set is not asked for them when requesting questions or content.
# Every answer that relies on context states the assumption in plain words.
# The teacher can correct an assumption in conversation, and the correction is used next time.
# A stated preference ("always include Spanish") is applied in a later, separate conversation.
# "What do you remember about me?" lists everything Scout remembers about the teacher.
# The teacher can open a view of what Scout remembers, edit or delete any item, and deleted items no longer affect answers.
# When classroom details are blank, Scout asks once, remembers the answer and does not ask again.
# Nothing remembered for one teacher appears for another, including a co-teacher of the same class.
# Nothing about individual students is remembered under this ticket.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Classroom subjects and dates are sometimes blank or placeholder values.
* Where "What Scout knows about me" appears is a Product design decision; it is a new element and must not change the approved Scout design.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-03: Teacher-Confirmed Actions
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Foundation

*Objective:* Let Scout move from suggesting to doing, while the teacher stays in charge of every change. One consistent confirm-before-acting pattern covers every action Scout takes, now and in later tickets.

*Problem:* Scout can suggest things, but the teacher still does the clicking across pages. Its report buttons describe where a report lives instead of opening it. Scout already asks for approval before some page actions; this makes that the single way every action works.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks for something to be done; Scout shows exactly what will happen, to whom and when, and waits.
* The teacher confirms, edits first, or declines.
* The teacher can see a list of what Scout has done and undo where the platform allows.
* Example requests: "Assign a 4-question quiz on Tools and Safety to the 3 students who scored below 60%.", "Create this assignment and assign it to my Period 3 class.", "Open the gradebook filtered to students under 60%.", "Save this leveled version and give it to Dolly.", "Open the Assessment Score report."

*Scope:*

* _Confirm-before-acting pattern (former 12.1, which absorbed brief 1.4):_ clear preview, explicit confirmation, a visible record of actions, undo where possible.
* _First actions:_ create an assignment draft; assign to a class or selected students; save a leveled or customised copy; open a page or report with filters set, rather than describing where it is.
* Later tickets (SCOUT-08, 09, 12, 14) add actions through the same pattern.
* Actions only on classes and students the teacher teaches.

*Out of scope:*

* Any action without confirmation, including scheduled or background actions.
* Sending messages to families or anyone else.
* Deleting data.
* Administrator actions.

*Depends on:* None. It builds on Scout's existing approval step and unlocks SCOUT-08, 09, 12 and 14.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Every action shows a preview naming what will change, for whom and when, before anything happens.
# Declining or closing the preview changes nothing.
# The teacher can edit the preview (for example students or due date) before confirming, and the result matches the edited preview.
# After confirming, the teacher sees what was done, with a link to it.
# A list of Scout's actions is visible to the teacher, each showing what was done, when and for whom.
# Where an action can be undone, the teacher can undo it from that list; where it cannot, the preview says so before the teacher confirms.
# Asking Scout to open a report or page opens it, with filters when asked, instead of describing where it is.
# Scout declines to act on a class or student the teacher does not teach, and says why.
# Scout never deletes data and never sends a message.
# No action happens without the teacher's confirmation, even when the request says "just do it".

*Risks / open questions:*

* Some changes cannot be reversed on the platform (for example, an assignment cannot be changed once a student has started it). The preview must say so plainly.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-04: Student Performance Insights From Any Page
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Foundation

*Objective:* Create one shared understanding of how each student and class is doing (scores, trends, missing and late work, activity) that Scout, reports and later features all draw on. Its first visible uses are Scout answers from any page and report summaries.

*Problem:* Scout offers "Who needs help" and "How is my class doing", but only when a report is on screen. From Teacher Notes, Scout said the page had no student data. The facts are spread over seven report tabs, the gradebook, the Grade queue and the bell, and reports hold the facts but no reading of them.

*Expected behaviour:*

* From any page, the teacher asks who needs help and gets a short ranked list across their classes, each student with a plain reason ("assessment scores fell from 82% to 54% over two weeks; two activities not submitted") and a link to the work. Scout says which classes and dates it looked at.
* On a report tab or the gradebook, the teacher reads a short summary of what stands out and can ask about it ("What did Maya get wrong here?").
* Example requests: "Who is falling behind in my Period 3 class?", "Which students have missing work this week?", "Who has improved since last month?", "Which students frequently submit late?", "Give me a two-paragraph summary of Week 1 for my principal."

*Scope:*

* _Shared student intelligence (former 2.1, with brief 2.4 and 2.5):_ overall performance and trend per student and class; missing work, late submissions, inactivity and declining participation; questions across every class the teacher owns or co-teaches; starts with what reports already show; definitions of "behind", "improving" and "inactive" recorded as placeholders.
* _Student questions from any page (former 1.1):_ answered anywhere; every named student comes with reason and evidence; report references open the report (through SCOUT-03); the "Needs a report" limitation is removed for these tools.
* _Report and gradebook summaries (former 2.3):_ a short summary on each report tab and the gradebook (what stands out, who is behind, what changed since last week); questions about the report; plain explanations of each measure; a copyable class-level summary for a colleague or principal, without names unless asked.

*Out of scope:*

* Question-type analysis and student profiles (SCOUT-10); standards mastery (SCOUT-11).
* Comparisons with other teachers, classes or schools.
* Any administrator view.
* Changing the layout of existing reports; any summary area is a new element agreed with Product.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01; SCOUT-03 for opening reports.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# "Which students need my help the most?" returns a useful answer from every teacher page tested, not a statement that the page has no student data.
# Each named student has a plain reason and a link to the work behind it.
# Every answer states which classes and date range it covers and how recent the information is.
# A teacher with several classes can ask once and get an answer across all of them.
# Answers include only classes the teacher owns or co-teaches; asked about another class, Scout says the teacher does not have access.
# Students removed from a class do not appear in its answers.
# The same question asked in Scout and read from a report summary gives the same students and figures.
# Every statement in a report summary can be traced to the table on the same page.
# When there is nothing to flag (for example no missing work), Scout says so plainly.
# Teachers checking a sample agree with who is flagged and why.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Report information is refreshed periodically, so answers may lag by minutes.
* Several engagement measures (highlights, crossword and misspelled time) have no stated meaning; no conclusions rest on them until Product defines them. Time spent on a question may not be recorded at all.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-05: Unified Content Discovery and Teaching Sets
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Foundation

*Objective:* Let Scout find anything a teacher can use, from a plain description, across every publication the teacher has, and assemble it into a set for a teaching task. Scout already finds teacher resources and media with previews and a choice of edition, and finds articles, vocabulary and questions in the open publication; this ticket extends that to everything the teacher can open.

*Problem:* SWO search is literal and split into four tabs; "photosynthesis" returned nothing in all four. Scout does better but stays tied to the publication on screen and asks the teacher to switch. A teacher who does not know the right words ("how plants make food") finds nothing. Assembling one lesson means finding an article, a video, questions, a printable and the standards one search at a time, and organizers are rarely found at all.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher describes a need and gets the best matches across their publications, grouped by type, each with a one-line reason, grade and publication. Content the school does not have is clearly marked.
* The teacher asks for materials for a topic and gets a teaching set: article, short video, lesson plan and resources, questions, vocabulary, a suitable graphic organizer and the standards covered, each explained. The teacher can remove items, ask for alternatives, and send the set to lesson preparation or assignment drafting.
* Example requests: "Something about how plants make food from sunlight, grade 4.", "A video under 3 minutes about the water cycle, Spanish if possible.", "Anything aligned to 4-LS1-1.", "Which of my publications covers ecosystems?", "Swap the video for something shorter."

*Scope:*

* _Unified discovery (former 3.1, with brief 1.2, 3.1, 3.4 and 4.4):_ plain-language requests across articles, lesson plans, teacher resources, media, questions, vocabulary, organizers and standards; every publication the teacher has, from any page; classroom grade, subject and state as defaults (SCOUT-02); finding by standard; honest access handling (SCOUT-01); Scout is the first place it appears; existing previews and edition choice kept.
* _Teaching sets (former 3.2):_ grouped sets organised around a teaching task; graphic organizer recommendations based on the lesson and content; refine by conversation; hand-off to SCOUT-08 and SCOUT-09.
* _Overlap note:_ Publication/unit/week filtering for teacher resources and media is already tracked in ONLINE-7492 — do not restate that rag filter work as new scope; SCOUT-05 covers unified discovery across content types and teaching sets beyond that.

*Out of scope:*

* Replacing the current Search page (approved design); recommending publications to buy; content from outside Studies Weekly.
* Pre-filled or newly generated organizers.
* Matching content to individual students (SCOUT-12).

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01. Better with SCOUT-02 and SCOUT-07.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# On a set of real teacher requests collected before testing, most return the content a teacher would have chosen, against a bar agreed before the run.
# Content in another of the teacher's publications is returned without the teacher first switching the open publication.
# Each result shows its type, grade, publication and a one-line reason it matched.
# Content in a publication the teacher's school does not have is never presented as available.
# A request by standard code returns content linked to that standard, or says none is linked.
# A teaching-set request returns items grouped by type, including an organizer where one fits, each with its reason.
# The teacher can remove an item or ask for an alternative, and the rest of the set is kept.
# Resource and media previews and the choice of edition still work as before.
# When nothing relevant exists, Scout says so, following SCOUT-01.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Some teacher resources and standards correlations exist only as PDFs, and some media has no transcript; these will be harder to find until they are prepared.
* The set of real teacher requests used for testing must be collected before work starts.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-06: Grading Assistance for Written Answers
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Strengthen Existing

*Objective:* Deliver the largest direct time saving in the audit. Grading suggestions for written answers are already built but hidden from teachers; this ticket validates and releases them, and adds grouping so similar answers are graded once.

*Problem:* Written-answer grading is the most repetitive task on the platform. The audit account had 103 items waiting, some three to four months old. Every answer, including nonsense like "gfsggdgd", needs a click and a score. When nine students gave essentially the same answer, the teacher still grades nine times.

*Expected behaviour:*

* Beside each answer the teacher sees a suggestion ("Partially correct, 1 of 2. Mentions the cause but not the effect"), the relevant phrase highlighted and a draft comment at the student's level, and accepts, edits or rejects it.
* Answers that need a closer human look (off-topic, very short, possibly concerning) are shown first, without any judgement attached.
* The teacher groups similar answers ("9 answers say plants get food from soil"), reviews each group, removes any that do not belong, and grades the rest together.
* Example requests: "Suggest marks for this question.", "Why did you suggest partially correct?", "Show me the answers you're least sure about first.", "Group the answers to Question 3.", "Grade this group as correct."

*Scope:*

* _Suggested grading (former 6.1):_ suggested mark, score, reason, highlighted evidence and draft feedback; a clear sign of how confident each suggestion is; teacher always confirms; checked against a set of teacher-graded answers before release, with the agreement bar set before the check; released to volunteer classrooms first.
* _Similar response grouping (former 6.2):_ group written answers by meaning; every answer stays visible; move answers out of a group; grade a reviewed group together; works alongside suggestions.

*Out of scope:*

* Drawings and handwriting (SCOUT-15).
* Saving any grade without the teacher; grading a group the teacher has not opened.
* Adjusting suggestions to an individual teacher's past marking.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# No grade is saved until the teacher confirms it, individually or for a group they have reviewed.
# Each suggestion shows a mark, score, reason, highlighted evidence and draft feedback.
# Each suggestion shows how confident it is.
# The teacher can accept, edit or reject each suggestion, and the grade saved is the one the teacher confirmed.
# Off-topic, nonsense or very short answers are shown first, with neutral wording.
# Before release, suggestions agree with teachers' own marks on a teacher-graded set at the level set before the check, and the result is recorded.
# Grouping shows every answer in each group, and the teacher can move an answer out before grading.
# Grading a group applies only to the answers in it at that moment.
# Where a question has little or no expected answer to grade against, the suggestion says so.
# Only teachers of the class can see suggestions for its answers.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Many questions have a short suggested answer and no rubric; suggestions will be weaker there.
* What happens beyond "shown first" for a possibly concerning answer needs a policy decision.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-08: Assignment Creation: Draft, Check and Reuse
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Strengthen Existing

*Objective:* Evolve today's one-question-at-a-time generator into whole-assignment drafting, with a quality check before anything goes out and help reusing what the teacher has already built.

*Problem:* Scout generates questions from a four-field form, but title, instructions, question mix, points, answer keys, standards and due date are still assembled by hand, about 20 minutes per assignment. Once any student starts an assignment it cannot be changed, so a wrong answer key is found too late. The audit account had 112 inactive assignments with names like "FIB - Blank - 1"; reusing last year's work means rebuilding it.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher describes an assignment and gets a complete draft: title, student instructions, questions, answer keys, points, suggested standards and due date, based on the right article. The teacher edits and saves; nothing is assigned until the teacher confirms.
* Before assigning, SWO lists things to check ("Question 3 may have two correct answers. Question 5 has no answer key. The passage reads above Grade 3."), each with a suggested fix. The teacher fixes, ignores or assigns anyway.
* The teacher asks for a past assignment; Scout finds it, shows how students did last time, and offers an editable copy.
* Example requests: "Create a 5-question exit ticket on Tools and Safety: two multiple choice, two short answer, one open response.", "Add two harder questions at the end.", "Check this quiz before I assign it.", "Reuse my Mindsets quiz from last year and update it for this week's article.", "Help me clean up my old test assignments."

*Scope:*

* _Full drafts (former 5.1):_ from a plain request, grounded in SWO content; question types SWO already supports; answer keys, points and suggested standards (SCOUT-07); defaults from SCOUT-02; saved as an editable draft.
* _Quality review (former 5.2):_ ambiguous or poor questions, duplicates, missing or doubtful answer keys, reading-level concerns and standards gaps against what the teacher intended; on hand-made and Scout-made assignments; advisory only.
* _Assignment library (former 5.4):_ find past assignments by description; copy and update for a new class, week or article; show how it went last time; suggest clearer names, near-duplicates and items to archive, each confirmed through SCOUT-03.

*Out of scope:*

* Differentiated versions (SCOUT-12); new question types.
* Automatic fixes; checking Studies Weekly's published assessments.
* Sharing assignments between teachers; deleting anything.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-03, SCOUT-05. Better with SCOUT-02 and SCOUT-07.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# A plain request produces a complete draft with title, instructions, questions, answer keys, points and suggested standards, using the count and mix of question types asked for.
# The draft is saved as a draft only and is not assigned until the teacher confirms a preview.
# The teacher can edit any part of the draft before saving.
# When a drawing question is included, the teacher is told it cannot yet receive grading help.
# The quality check runs before assigning on both hand-made and Scout-made assignments; each concern names the question, the problem and a suggested fix.
# The teacher can fix, ignore or assign anyway; no concern changes the assignment by itself.
# An assignment with no problems gets a clear "nothing to check" rather than invented concerns.
# A past assignment can be found by description in one request, with last time's results where they exist.
# A copy is a new draft; the original is unchanged.
# Renames and archiving happen only after confirmation; nothing is deleted.
# A content-team review of a sample finds generated questions accurate and grade-appropriate.

*Risks / open questions:*

* What counts as "above grade level" or a "poor question" is a placeholder until the curriculum and content team sets it.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-09: Pacing, Lesson Preparation and Week Planning
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Near-Term

*Objective:* Remove the "where were we?" step, turn a dozen resource sections into one page, and keep the plan realistic when the year changes. Scout can already draft lesson and week plans and "Plan next week", but these are not yet available to all teachers, need the table of contents open, and cover one publication.

*Problem:* Publication cards say nothing about progress or what comes next. Preparing one week means reading 13 or more teacher-resource sections, several of them PDFs, plus finding the article, video and questions. When a class loses a week to testing, the plan is rebuilt by hand, if at all.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks where a class is and hears, for example, "By your calendar you should be in Week 6 of 32; the class has finished Week 4. Next up is Week 5: Forces and Motion."
* The teacher asks for help preparing and gets a one-page pack: objective, standards in plain words, background, a sequence sized to the time available, the article and video, a few questions, a suitable organizer, what to print and reading versions, each linked to its source.
* The teacher asks to replan and sees what to combine, shorten or mark optional, with reasons; after confirmation Scout applies the changes, which can be reverted.
* Example requests: "Where are we in Science?", "I'm teaching photosynthesis tomorrow. I have 30 minutes. Help me prepare.", "Plan my next two weeks across Science and Well-Being.", "We lost a week to testing. Rebuild the plan so we finish by June.", "Help a student who was absent last week catch up."

*Scope:*

* _Pacing awareness (former 9.1, with brief 9.4):_ expected versus actual position per class and publication from the classroom's dates; the suggested next lesson; from any page.
* _Lesson preparation (former 9.2, with brief 3.3):_ a pack for a topic, article, week or date; sized to the time available; every part cites its SWO source; organizer and reading-version suggestions where available.
* _Week planning and catch-up (former 9.3, with brief 9.2):_ plans across one or more publications against the class calendar; catch-up for a class or one student; visibility and order changes applied only after confirmation (SCOUT-03) and reversible.

*Out of scope:*

* Speaker notes or edited slide decks; content from outside Studies Weekly.
* Any change without the teacher's confirmation.
* School or district pacing guides; holidays beyond what the teacher tells Scout.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-03, SCOUT-04, SCOUT-05. Better with SCOUT-02 and SCOUT-07.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Asked where a class is, Scout states the expected and actual position and the next lesson, from any page.
# When class dates or progress are missing or look like placeholders, Scout says so and asks rather than guessing.
# Pacing statements agree wherever they appear (Scout, prep packs, plans).
# A prep pack fits the time given, and every statement in it links to the SWO source it came from.
# The teacher can edit the pack.
# A replan shows each proposed change with its reason before anything is applied.
# Nothing in the publication changes until the teacher confirms, and every applied change can be undone.
# A plan can span more than one publication.
# Where skipping an item would drop a linked standard, the plan says so; where standards are not linked, it says it cannot check.

*Risks / open questions:*

* The Progress Report on the audit account showed almost every week "Not Started", which may reflect classes taught partly offline. Product must define what "progress" means before pacing can be trusted.
* Suggested lesson sequences follow placeholder teaching rules until the curriculum team reviews them.
* Item length and standards information may be incomplete, limiting what Scout can judge as safe to skip.

Welcome to Second Grade — Weekly Plan
Week overview
Grade: 2
Subject: Social Studies
Week's goal: Students will learn about American symbols (the American Flag and the Bald Eagle), practice reciting the Pledge of Allegiance and the Pledge to the Texas Flag, and discuss the importance of being honest.
Standards: Linked to this week (not a focus of this plan): Standards004.pdf, TX2-Scope-and-Sequence-TEKS-Update.pdf.
Materials across the week: Welcome to Second Grade, Important Words and Their Meanings, The Pledge of Allegiance, Honesty, Pledge to the Texas Flag, The Bald Eagle, American Stories, Write a Sentence, and A Pledge is a Promise (all from this week's articles); Vocabulary panel (allegiance, indivisible, justice, liberty, pledge, republic); Weekly assessment built from this week's assessment questions.

This week has nine short articles and one vocabulary panel rather than a small handful of terms, so the plan below groups articles by theme across five days instead of spreading them thin — each day pairs a reading with a related activity so all nine articles are covered.

Day 1 — Starting the Year and Learning Key Words
Objective (Scout's draft): Students will identify that this year's social studies will cover their community, state, country, and world, and will begin learning the meanings of republic, indivisible, liberty, and justice.

Read/use: Welcome to Second Grade; Important Words and Their Meanings; Vocabulary panel.

Steps:

Read aloud Welcome to Second Grade. Ask students what topics they will learn about this year (community, state, country, world).
Read aloud Important Words and Their Meanings. Pause after each sentence to say the term and its meaning together as a class.
Show the four vocabulary cards (republic, indivisible, liberty, justice) and have students repeat each word and definition chorally.
Have students draw a simple picture for one word (for example, a scale for justice, an unbroken chain for indivisible) and label it with the word.
Quick check: Ask each student to say one vocabulary word and its meaning in their own words as an exit check.

Day 2 — The Pledge of Allegiance
Objective (Scout's draft): Students will recite the Pledge of Allegiance and explain what it means to pledge allegiance to the flag.

Read/use: The Pledge of Allegiance; A Pledge is a Promise; Vocabulary panel (pledge, allegiance).

Steps:

Read aloud A Pledge is a Promise. Discuss: what is a pledge? (a promise) What are you promising when you pledge allegiance to the flag? (to be loyal to the flag and your country)
Read aloud The Pledge of Allegiance together, pointing to each word.
Practice reciting the Pledge as a class two or three times, standing as usual for the Pledge.
Turn to a partner and explain in one sentence what "pledge" means, using the vocabulary definition (a pledge is a promise).
Quick check: Listen as students recite the Pledge together; note whether each student can say the words "pledge" and "allegiance" and explain what a pledge is.

Day 3 — Pledge to the Texas Flag and the Idea of "Indivisible"
Objective (Scout's draft): Students will recite the Pledge to the Texas Flag and connect the word "indivisible" to both pledges.

Read/use: Pledge to the Texas Flag; Vocabulary panel (indivisible, republic).

Steps:

Review the meaning of indivisible from Day 1 (our country cannot be divided or separated).
Read aloud Pledge to the Texas Flag together.
Practice reciting the Texas Pledge as a class.
Compare: find the word "indivisible" in the Pledge of Allegiance and "one and indivisible" in the Texas Pledge. Ask students what they notice is similar between the two pledges.
Students copy or trace the Texas Pledge on paper as handwriting practice.
Quick check: Have students recite the Texas Pledge and point to the word that means "cannot be divided" when asked.

Day 4 — Honesty, the Bald Eagle, and American Stories
Objective (Scout's draft): Students will explain why being honest is important, describe why the bald eagle was chosen as an American symbol, and preview this year's American Stories feature.

Read/use: Honesty; The Bald Eagle; American Stories.

Steps:

Read aloud Honesty. Discuss the question in the article: "What are some other ways you can be a good citizen?" List student answers on the board.
Read aloud The Bald Eagle. Discuss: what did Benjamin Franklin think the national symbol should be (the turkey), and why did other people prefer the bald eagle (it was strong and brave)?
Ask: what does the bald eagle represent in the United States? (strength and bravery)
Read aloud American Stories to preview that students will learn about American heroes this year.
Students draw a bald eagle and write one word that it represents (strength or bravery).
Quick check: Ask students to tell a partner one reason people chose the bald eagle as America's symbol, and one way to be a good citizen.

Day 5 — Write a Sentence and Weekly Assessment
Objective (Scout's draft): Students will write sentences about the bald eagle and about being a good citizen, then complete the weekly assessment.

Read/use: Write a Sentence; Weekly assessment built from this week's assessment questions.

Steps:

Reread The Bald Eagle aloud as a refresher.
Read the prompts in Write a Sentence: explain why the bald eagle was a good choice for our American symbol, and write a sentence about how to be a good citizen.
Students write their two sentences independently; circulate to support students who need help getting started.
Share a few sentences aloud as volunteers wish.
Weekly assessment: administer the assessment for this week.
Quick check: Review student sentences for a clear reason (strength/bravery) and a clear idea about good citizenship before the assessment begins.

Standards
Linked to this week (not a focus of this plan): Standards004.pdf, TX2-Scope-and-Sequence-TEKS-Update.pdf.

Differentiation
Vocabulary support: Pair the five key words (allegiance, indivisible, justice, liberty, pledge, republic) with the picture cards made on Day 1 for students who benefit from visual supports; keep these visible all week for reference during the Pledges and the assessment.
Oral rehearsal: For both Pledges, let students who need more practice echo phrase-by-phrase behind the teacher or a peer before joining the whole group recitation.
Writing supports: On Day 5, offer a sentence starter ("The bald eagle was a good choice because...", "I can be a good citizen by...") for students who need help beginning independent writing; allow students who are ready to write an additional sentence.
Discussion depth: During Day 4's honesty and citizenship discussion, invite students who are ready for more challenge to give two reasons instead of one, while others can respond with a single word or short phrase.

*Improvements:*


{noformat}1. [High] The top-level "Built for" objective doesn't represent the whole week
The card header says: "Built for: Scout's draft: Students will identify that this year's social studies will cover their community, state, country, and world, and will begin learning the meanings of republic, indivisible, liberty, and justice." That's word-for-word Day 1's objective, not a whole-week summary. Meanwhile the "Week overview" section separately states the real week-level goal: "Students will learn about American symbols (the American Flag and the Bald Eagle), practice reciting the Pledge of Allegiance and the Pledge to the Texas Flag, and discuss the importance of being honest." These two don't match — a teacher skimming just the top card would get no sense that the week covers the flag, the eagle, or either pledge at all, since that top line only reflects Day 1's narrower vocabulary-focused objective. Worth checking whether the "Built for" field is supposed to pull a week-level summary and is grabbing Day 1's objective by mistake.

2. [Medium] Differentiation section miscounts the vocabulary words
"Vocabulary support: Pair the five key words (allegiance, indivisible, justice, liberty, pledge, republic)..." — that's six words listed, not five. It does match the Materials section's vocabulary panel count (6 words: 4 from Day 1, 2 from Day 2), so the list itself is right — just the number "five" is wrong.

3. [Low] The Standards note is repeated verbatim in two places
"Linked to this week (not a focus of this plan): Standards004.pdf, TX2-Scope-and-Sequence-TEKS-Update.pdf." appears identically in the Week overview and again in its own Standards section further down. Not wrong, just redundant — could be stated once.

4. [Low, worth a quick sanity check] The title "Welcome to Second Grade — Weekly Plan" appears three times (the chat announcement, the plan card, and the page heading). This is most likely just the normal card-then-full-document structure rather than a bug, but given the exact-duplicate-content issue flagged in the pacing plan reviewed earlier in this thread, it's worth a quick confirmation that this is intentional layering and not the same kind of double-render.{noformat}

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-10: Student Profiles, Question-Type Patterns and Family Drafts
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Medium-Term

*Objective:* Give teachers a quick, fair picture of an individual student when time is shortest (conferences, intervention meetings), reveal patterns hidden inside mixed averages, and turn that picture into communication the teacher controls.

*Problem:* Building a picture of one student means paging through 32 weeks of a report, ten rows at a time, across three sections. One average mixes every question type, so a student who does well on multiple choice but struggles to explain in writing looks average. Family updates are written by hand, often in two languages, and this is where a careless sentence about a child does the most harm.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks for a student summary and gets recent results, strengths, areas to work on, engagement changes ("activity dropped after Week 12") and two or three talking points, each linked to the work, all editable.
* The teacher asks about question types and sees results per type with the number of questions behind each figure.
* The teacher asks for a family update and gets a warm, specific draft built only from that student's records, in the language the teacher chooses, to copy into their usual channel.
* Example requests: "Summarize Arthur for a parent conference.", "Which students do well on multiple choice but poorly on open response?", "What changed for Dolly in the last three weeks?", "Draft a short update for Arthur's family, in English and Spanish.", "Give me a two-paragraph summary of Week 1 for my principal."

*Scope:*

* _Question-type performance (former 2.2):_ by question type for a class, group or student; the number of questions always shown; available from any page.
* _Student profile (former 2.4):_ strengths, gaps, trends, engagement and suggested next steps, each with evidence; editable conference talking points.
* _Family and administrator drafts (former 12.2):_ drafts for one family, all families or an administrator; a family draft uses only that student's information; Spanish when the teacher asks; administrator summaries are class-level with no names unless asked; the teacher sends outside SWO.

*Out of scope:*

* SWO sending messages, emails or texts.
* Student-facing or administrator-facing profiles.
* Labels, diagnoses, predictions, rankings or comparisons with classmates.
* Explaining why students got questions wrong (SCOUT-14); changing how any question type is scored.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01, SCOUT-04. Better with SCOUT-06 (more graded written answers) and SCOUT-11.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# A student summary is available from any page, and every statement in it links to its evidence.
# Talking points and drafts are editable before use.
# Every question-type figure shows how many questions it rests on; where there are too few to judge, Scout says so instead of reporting a pattern.
# The "good at multiple choice, weak at open response" question is answered in one request.
# A family draft mentions no other student and makes no comparison with classmates.
# Scout uses Spanish only when the teacher asks; it does not guess a family's language.
# An administrator summary contains no student names unless the teacher asks for them.
# SWO never sends a draft; the teacher copies it.
# A reviewer reading a sample of profiles and drafts finds no labels, diagnoses or predictions.
# A teacher cannot get a profile of a student outside their classes.
# For a student with little recorded work, Scout says there is not enough to summarise.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Open-response and drawing scores exist only once graded (103 items were waiting on the audit account), and drawings are marked against "Drawings will vary"; these results stay thin until grading keeps pace.
* Family contact details are incomplete and should not be needed; any future sending would need its own consent and privacy review.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-11: Standards Coverage and Mastery
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Medium-Term

*Objective:* Connect standards to students without the teacher reading the whole Standards Report matrix, and give a clear view of coverage before the end of the year. Topic questions work too, by unit or week where no standard is linked.

*Problem:* The Standards Report matrix is useful but has many columns and no reading of it. Teachers cannot easily answer "what have I not covered this quarter?" or "which standard is weakest?", and topic-level questions ("who struggles with fractions?") have no home.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks which standards the class is weakest on and gets the two or three weakest, the class result on each, the students furthest behind and how many questions sit behind each figure.
* For a topic with no standards linked, Scout answers by unit or week and says so.
* Example requests: "Which standards have I not covered this quarter?", "Who is struggling with 4-PS3-2?", "Which students struggle with map skills?", "What standards remain before the end of the year?"

*Scope:*

* _Coverage (former 4.3, with brief 4.2):_ what has been taught and assessed, and what remains, for a chosen period.
* _Mastery by standard and topic (former 4.3, with brief 2.3 and 4.3):_ for the class and for students; question counts always shown; answers from any page; unit or week fallback for topics.

*Out of scope:*

* Grades or official mastery determinations.
* What content to use next (SCOUT-14).
* Comparisons with other classes or schools.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-04, SCOUT-07.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Coverage for a chosen period (covered, assessed, remaining) is answered in one request.
# The weakest standards are listed with the class result and the students furthest behind, each figure with its question count.
# A standard is never called weak on too few questions; Scout says there is not enough evidence.
# Where a publication has no linked standards, Scout says so and answers by unit or week where it can.
# Figures agree with the Standards Report for the same class and period.
# Results that rest on links not yet confirmed by the content team are marked.
# No result is described as a grade or an official mastery determination.
# Only the teacher's own classes are included.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Results are only as complete as the standards links from SCOUT-07.
* The threshold for "weak" is a placeholder until the curriculum team sets it.
