column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-12: Differentiation: Groups, Matched Readers and Versions
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Medium-Term

*Objective:* Make differentiation realistic at class scale using content and supports SWO already has. Scout can already level an article, but the teacher has to choose the level; this ticket lets the evidence suggest it, with the teacher deciding.

*Problem:* Grouping is done from memory or not at all. Differentiating means building several assignments by hand. Leveled readers come in Above, Approaching and On versions in English and Spanish, and nothing says which student should get which. Each student has six support switches, usually left at defaults.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks for groups for a lesson and gets three or four with the reason for each; the teacher moves students and renames groups.
* The teacher asks which reader each student should get and sees a list by version, with evidence, to adjust and then print or assign after confirming.
* The teacher asks for versions of a quiz and gets more-support, on-level and extension versions with proposed students; nothing is assigned until confirmed.
* Where usage evidence exists, SWO suggests an existing support ("Three students replay article audio often; you might consider Audio Reader").
* Example requests: "Group my class for Tuesday's lesson on fractions.", "Which reader should Dolly get?", "Make an easier version of this for students who scored under 60%.", "Print Spanish versions for my English learners.", "Would any students benefit from Time Delay?"

*Scope:*

* _Flexible groups (former 8.2):_ temporary, teacher-owned groups for a stated purpose, with evidence; reused by the parts below.
* _Matched readers and versions (former 8.1, with brief 8.3):_ leveled reader per student per unit; the level for Scout's article leveling suggested from results; Spanish when the teacher chooses.
* _Differentiated assignments (former 5.3):_ versions at different levels of support; placements with evidence, teacher-adjustable; each version assigned after confirmation (SCOUT-03).
* _Support suggestions (former 8.3):_ existing supports only (Audio Reader, Time Delay, Vocabulary Definitions and others) with the usage evidence behind them; the teacher turns them on; the teacher can stop a kind of suggestion. This part is released only after policy review, and only if the usage evidence is recorded.

*Out of scope:*

* Placing students or changing supports without confirmation.
* Permanent ability tracks; group names, levels or scores visible to students or families.
* New readers or supports; groups shared across teachers.
* Any suggestion implying a disability, diagnosis or special-education need.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01, SCOUT-03, SCOUT-04, SCOUT-08.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Each suggested group has a reason drawn from recent work; the teacher can move students, rename or discard groups.
# Groups are never visible to students or families.
# Each reader recommendation shows its evidence and is never described as a reading-level diagnosis.
# Scout chooses Spanish versions only when the teacher asks.
# Differentiated versions show the proposed students and reasons; nothing is assigned until confirmed, and each student receives only their version.
# Version names that students see are neutral.
# Where Scout has too little evidence to place a student, it says so and leaves the choice to the teacher.
# Support suggestions appear only with usage evidence; when none is recorded, no suggestion appears.
# No support setting changes unless the teacher turns it on, and a dismissed kind of suggestion stops appearing.
# A reviewer reading a sample finds no labels about children.

*Risks / open questions:*

* SWO has no direct reading-level measure; levels are inferred from question results, a weak signal. Matching rules are placeholders for the curriculum team.
* The audit saw leveled readers for Kindergarten to Grade 2 only.
* The audit could not confirm that audio replays, word look-ups or pauses are recorded; if not, the support part waits. It also needs policy review before release.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-13: Daily Briefing and Notification Digest
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Medium-Term (notification grouping can start earlier on simple rules)

*Objective:* Replace the walk across six screens per class with one short read, and turn a long notification list into a few actionable groups. This is the first place teachers meet AI without asking, so it draws only on intelligence already validated in earlier tickets.

*Problem:* The home page carries no information about students. The answer to "what needs me today?" is spread across the bell, the Grade queue, four report tabs and the gradebook, repeated for each class. The audit account had 274 notifications over 14 pages, mostly repeated "N submissions, teacher grading required" lines, with no sign of which were stale, and each was a link rather than an action.

*Expected behaviour:*

* On opening SWO the teacher reads, for example: "12 items waiting to be graded, oldest 3 months. Two students in Period 3 missed the last three activities. Science is two weeks behind your calendar. Next up: Week 5, Forces and Motion." Each line has one action, and each class has a one-line health summary.
* The bell shows a few groups instead of many lines ("5 items waiting to be graded in Period 3, oldest 3 months: Grade now").
* Example requests: "What changed since Friday?", "Which class needs me most this week?", "What's important in my notifications?", "Show me the briefing for Period 2 only.", "What did I miss this week?"

*Scope:*

* _Daily briefing (former 10.1, with brief 10.2):_ grading waiting, students needing attention, missing work, pacing and upcoming items; a one-line summary per class; each finding with evidence and one action. Where it appears is a Product design decision; approved layouts do not change without sign-off.
* _Notification grouping and digest (former 10.2, brief 10.3):_ group by class and type, remove duplicates, rank by urgency and age; each group links to its action; a weekly in-product summary.

*Out of scope:*

* Emails or messages to teachers.
* Any action taken without the teacher.
* Deleting notifications.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01, SCOUT-03, SCOUT-04, SCOUT-09 (pacing). Notification grouping alone needs none of these.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# The briefing covers grading waiting, students needing attention, missing work, pacing and upcoming items, each finding with its evidence and one action.
# Each class has a one-line summary.
# Figures in the briefing match what Scout and the reports say for the same question.
# When nothing needs attention, the briefing says so briefly.
# Each action opens the right place in one click; nothing changes without confirmation.
# Repeated notifications collapse into one group with a count and the age of the oldest item.
# Groups are ordered by urgency and age.
# The weekly summary appears in the product only; no email is sent.
# Original notifications remain reachable; none are deleted.
# Only the teacher's own classes appear.

*Risks / open questions:*

* A briefing built on untrustworthy findings is the most visible way to lose teacher trust; it should not release before SCOUT-04 has passed teacher review.
* "Upcoming items" needs a Product definition.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-14: Misconception Analysis and Reteaching Loop
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Medium-Term (the follow-up completes the loop last)

*Objective:* Take the teacher from "they got it wrong" to "here is what to do tomorrow", and then show whether it helped, in one flow. This ties student insights, content, assignment drafting and confirmed actions into a teaching routine.

*Problem:* Statistics show that scores are low but not why. The Snapshot Report needs three selections before it shows anything and never explains the result. After grading, patterns across answers stay in the teacher's head. Writing a reteach activity takes time, so reteaching happens for the whole class or not at all, and nothing tells the teacher whether it worked.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher asks why the class struggled and hears, for example, "Most students who missed it chose 'paint' as a tool. That may suggest confusion between tools and materials," with the answer counts. After grading: "7 of 25 students wrote that plants get food from soil."
* The teacher says "Reteach this" and gets a recommendation, existing SWO content, a short activity and the suggested students; the teacher edits and confirms before anything is assigned.
* Days later: "5 of 6 students who did the reteach set now answer this kind of question correctly. One still struggles; here is his work."
* Example requests: "Why did the class do poorly on Question 2?", "What did the class misunderstand in yesterday's article?", "Give me a five-minute review for what they missed.", "What content can I use for 4-PS3-2?", "Did the reteach on tools and materials work?"

*Scope:*

* _Misconception insights (former 7.1, with brief 6.3 grading insights):_ for multiple choice, which wrong answers were chosen and what that may suggest; for written answers, common misunderstandings found during grading and grouping; defaults to the most recently taught item; counts always shown; "may", not "does".
* _Reteach recommendations and activities (former 7.2, with brief 7.3 and 4.4):_ what to review, from a misconception or weak standard; existing SWO content for it; a generated activity of a few minutes; suggested students with evidence. Assessment-result grouping + short reteach suggestion is already in ONLINE-7498 — do not restate that slice; keep misconception insights, confirm-before-assign reteach flow, and close-the-loop follow-up as SCOUT-14 scope.
* _Close the loop (former 7.3):_ one continuous flow in Scout; a follow-up on the reteach results in Scout and in the briefing; every change confirmed.

*Out of scope:*

* Automatic interventions.
* Conclusions about individual students' abilities.
* Claims that the reteach caused an improvement; Scout reports before and after only.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-03, 04, 05, 06, 08, 10 and 13. Standards-based reteaching also needs SCOUT-11.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Every finding shows the counts behind it and uses "may", not "does".
# When there is no clear pattern, Scout says so.
# Written-answer patterns come only from graded answers and say how many were graded.
# A reteach recommendation names and links the SWO content it draws on.
# The activity is short and editable, the student list shows evidence, and nothing is assigned until the teacher confirms.
# The follow-up reports before and after for the students who did the activity and names those still struggling, with their work.
# The follow-up never says the reteach caused the improvement.
# The teacher can go from "who needs help" to an assigned reteach activity without leaving Scout.
# A content-team review of a sample finds activities accurate and on target.
# Only the teacher's own classes are included.

*Risks / open questions:*

* The audit could not confirm that SWO keeps which wrong answer each student chose; if not, multiple-choice analysis is limited to "missed or not" until it is recorded.
* How much reteaching a finding warrants is a placeholder for the curriculum team.
* Written-answer patterns stay thin until grading keeps pace (SCOUT-06).

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-15: Grading Drawings and Handwritten Responses
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Longer-Term

*Objective:* Carry the time saving of written-answer grading to question types common in the early grades, without pretending to mark what has no fair criteria. This follows only once SCOUT-06 is released and trusted.

*Problem:* Many activities ask students to draw ("Draw the tower you made"). These are graded entirely by hand, and their suggested answer is often "Drawings will vary", so there is nothing fair to mark against.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The teacher opens a drawing response and sees a short, neutral description of what it shows and, where the question has clear criteria, a suggested mark with the reason.
* Where criteria are missing, SWO describes only and says it cannot suggest a mark.
* For photographed handwriting, SWO shows what it read so the teacher can check it.
* Example requests: "Describe what these drawings show.", "Which drawings include the labels I asked for?", "Suggest marks for these diagrams.", "What does this handwritten answer say?"

*Scope:*

* _Drawings and handwriting (former 6.3):_ drawings first, then photographed handwriting; suggestions only where the question has clear criteria; the same teacher-confirms rule as SCOUT-06; checked against teachers' own marks before release; volunteer classrooms first.

*Out of scope:*

* Any release before SCOUT-06 is released and trusted.
* Judging artistic quality.
* Saving any grade without the teacher.

*Depends on:* SCOUT-01, SCOUT-06.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# For a drawing question with clear criteria, the suggestion includes a mark and a reason tied to those criteria.
# Where criteria are missing, SWO describes the drawing, declines to mark and says why.
# No grade is saved without the teacher's confirmation.
# Descriptions are neutral and never comment on artistic quality.
# For handwriting, SWO shows what it read before any suggestion; if it cannot read the answer, it says so.
# Before release, agreement with teachers' marks on drawings with clear criteria meets a bar set before the check.
# Teachers in the pilot report that it saves time.

*Risks / open questions:*

* Most drawing questions have no marking criteria; the content team would need to add them for this to be worthwhile.
* Young children's drawings and handwriting are hard to read, and mistakes are visible to families.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-H: Hints Match Current Step or Tab
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Strengthen Existing

*Objective:* Every suggestion Scout shows is something the teacher can act on right now, on the exact step or tab in front of them.

*Problem:* A browser audit of Scout's quick-suggestion chips and the "What Scout can do → On this page" list found them chosen by page, not by the step or tab within it:

* Step 1 of Create Classroom offers "Create the classroom" while its required fields are empty.
* The Customized Content builder offers Step 2 and Step 3 actions on Step 1.
* The article page's Grade and Highlights tabs show Student View's reading-level and answer-key hints.
* "Set Student Status" leaks from the Grade tab into Highlights.
* The Grade tab offers nothing about who has turned work in.

The table of contents, Publication Report, Highlights, Standards Report, Customized Content Report and Snapshot already get this right. Both surfaces read from the same place, so they are wrong together.

*Expected behaviour:*

* Each chip passes one test: could the teacher act on it right now, without navigating first?
* Page-wide items ("What is this page and what can I do here?", "Switch tab") stay on every view of the page.
* A later step's action never appears before its step.
* A tab built around one question offers that question: the Grade tab offers "Who hasn't turned this in?" and "Summarize how the class did".
* Navigation chips ("Next: add content", "Switch tab") look different from action chips (a muted, dashed style), so "go somewhere" is never mistaken for "do something here".
* Between 1 and 5 chips, only as many as genuinely fit.

*Scope:*

* *Customized Content builder, per step:*
** Step 1: help writing instructions, a due date, "What is this page", Next.
** Step 2: import, add a question, generate questions from an article, Next.
** Step 3: choose who gets it, a due date, Back.
* *Create Classroom, per step:*
** Step 1: fill in details, suggest start and end dates.
** Step 2: publications.
** Step 3: students, and the real "Create the classroom" action.
* *Article page, per tab:*
** Student View: unchanged.
** Grade: who hasn't turned it in, and a class summary. This is new data Scout can read on the Grade tab.
** Highlights: summarise highlights, and who highlighted least.
** Statistics: checked against what's on screen.
* *Reports tabs:* checked against the one-question test. Items already correct stay.
* *The "On this page" list* follows the same rule as the chips.
* *The navigation-chip style:* a new, muted look for navigation chips, approved by Salman as a change to the chip design.
* *Due-date suggestions:* use the app's existing scheduling logic if it exists. If there is nothing to base them on, they become a chat question Scout answers.

*Out of scope:* new Scout abilities beyond what these chips need; "Print this roster" (Scout cannot print); new report insights (SCOUT-04 / ONLINE-7510); changes to the table of contents or Publication Report hints.

*Depends on:* None.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# On every step of the Customized Content builder and Create Classroom, every chip and "On this page" card acts on what is on screen.
# No later-step action appears before its step; "Create the classroom" appears only on the last step.
# On the article Grade tab, "Who hasn't turned this in?" and "Summarize how the class did" appear and answer correctly from the roster on screen.
# On the Highlights tab, no Student View or Grade-tab chip appears.
# Navigation chips are visibly different from action chips.
# Each view shows at most 5 chips, and fewer where fewer fit.
# The table of contents and Publication Report show the same chips as before.
# Every chip shown works when clicked.

*Risks / open questions:* The audit did not reach some sub-views live (Create Classroom Steps 2–3, the Statistics tab, some reports); they are checked against the code and verified by hand.

column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Strengthen Existing

*Objective:* Make the Meet Scout tour feel smooth, accurate and interactive. The popup's look stays the same.

*Problem:* The tour uses the tour library's default thin ring around the target, with no dimming. The library's own mask is switched off, so the page is never dimmed and the target is never set apart. Moving between steps jumps rather than glides. The tour was modelled on the classroom intro, which shares the same tour component.

*Expected behaviour:*

* The page dims, and the element being explained sits in a clear, softly lit rectangular cut-out.
* Between steps, the spotlight and the popup glide together to the next target, which scrolls into view first.
* Resizing the window or scrolling keeps the spotlight and popup aligned.
* Esc closes the tour; the arrow keys move between steps; focus stays in the popup.
* For teachers who turn off motion, movement becomes simple fades.
* The popup's styling (look, text, buttons) is unchanged.

*Scope:*

* A spotlight engine modelled on the env-board guided tour: four dimming panels around a lit frame, moving together, with rules for scrolling into view and for phone vs desktop.
* The same engine positions the popup, so spotlight and popup move as one.
* It applies only to the Meet Scout tour; the classroom intro tour is unchanged.
* The tour stays on top of other overlays, as it does today.
* Every current tour target has been checked and is correct; they stay as they are.

*Out of scope:* the classroom intro tour's look; new tour steps or text; the popup's design.

*Depends on:* None.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Each step highlights exactly its element, with the rest of the page dimmed, and the element is scrolled into view.
# Moving between steps animates the spotlight and popup together, smoothly.
# Resizing or scrolling keeps them aligned with the target.
# Esc closes the tour, and the arrow keys move back and forward.
# With reduced motion switched on, transitions are simple fades.
# The popup looks as it does today.
# The tour appears above other overlays.
# The classroom intro tour is unchanged.

*Risks / open questions:* Targets inside Scout's own dialog and on the page behind it both need to line up; this is checked by hand on desktop and phone widths.

column5:

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-C: Shared response cache and cheaper labelling for Scout evaluation runs
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Technical housekeeping

*Objective:* Stop paying twice for the same AI request when Scout's behaviour is tested, and make every test run's cost visible before it runs.

*Problem:* Scripted Scout evaluations call Bedrock directly. Re-running an unchanged evaluation pays again for identical requests, and bulk labelling has used the most expensive model. One day of testing cost about $155 without a prior estimate.

*Expected behaviour:* Teachers see no change. Every evaluation script, labeller and calibration run goes through one shared record-and-replay cache, keyed by model and the full request, so an identical request is answered from disk at no cost. Measurement still uses the production models.

*Scope:*

* One shared record-and-replay cache used by default by every evaluation script, labeller and calibration run.
* Bulk labelling uses Sonnet, with an Opus spot-check where agreement must be proven.
* Bedrock batch jobs where answers are not needed immediately.
* A cost estimate printed before each run, the actual cost after it, and a per-day total.

*Out of scope:* Scout's own production prompt caching (covered by the cost-and-speed ticket); changing which models Scout uses in production.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Re-running an unchanged evaluation makes no new Bedrock calls.
# All existing evaluation scripts use the cache.
# Every run prints its estimated and actual cost, and a per-day total is kept.
# Bulk labelling can run as batch jobs at the lower price.
column6:
30/Sep/26 11:58 PM;712020:8d8291ea-ff3a-422f-9681-544160715a21;_QA: ONLINE-7525 (Shared response cache for Scout evaluation runs), local rag checkout on ONLINE-5385_scout_ai_integration (35b99fba), live Bedrock in us-west-2 (tester's AWS SSO session)_

No swo-3.0 change and no UI, so this was tested from a terminal, not on dev2. Teachers see no change: the Lambda imports nothing from {{experiments/}}.

_How it was tested:_ rag on {{ONLINE-5385_scout_ai_integration}} at {{35b99fba}} (contains ONLINE-7525 commits {{9d11e0d2}}, {{d3c400f8}}), dependencies installed with {{make install-dev}}. AWS access confirmed with {{aws sts get-caller-identity}} (SSO, us-west-2). Then {{SMOKE_LIVE=1 AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-west-2 bash ONLINE-7525-smoke-tests.sh}}: it runs the developer's three check scripts, then its own offline checks, prints a cost estimate, and makes 4 real Haiku 4.5 calls through the shared cache. Everything it writes goes to a temp folder that is deleted afterwards, so no real cache or ledger changed. Real Bedrock calls are counted by a wrapper outside the cache, so "no call" is measured independently of the cache's own report.

_Developer's check scripts (fake Bedrock client, no AWS):_ PASS 30/30

* {{check_bedrock_cache.py}} 14/14: a repeat request reaches Bedrock once; a changed message or model calls again; the original is still a hit afterwards; 16 simultaneous writers leave one valid file; {{replay}} raises on an unseen request without calling; {{record}} always calls; {{off}} always calls and counts nothing; {{invoke_model}} repeats are cached.
* {{check_cost_meter.py}} 11/11: estimates match hand-worked figures ($0.176 Sonnet, $0.11 Haiku), batch is half; actual cost from tokens in both Bedrock formats; prompt-cache tokens at their own rate; ledger totals and an empty day at $0; cost read back from cache files.
* {{check_bedrock_batch.py}} 5/5: refuses with no bucket or only a bucket; builds settings with both; a batch result written into the cache is found by a normal {{replay}} client.
* Weaker than their names: _"off mode wrote nothing new"_ checks counters, not files (live T5 covers it); _"invoke_model … different key order"_ sends the same order twice, so it only proves a plain repeat; the batch read-back uses a fake result already in {{converse}} format (finding 2).

_Smoke script, offline checks:_ PASS 7/8 (plus T1 above)

* Cache key ignores key order and changes with the prompt, temperature or model. An unknown {{BEDROCK_CACHE_MODE}} is refused. Each cache folder gets its own {{.gitignore}}.
* Estimate: 40 Sonnet calls at 1000 in / 200 out → _$0.176_, _$0.088_ as a batch job.
* Per-day ledger: _"2026-10-01: $0.3000 across 2 recorded run(s)"_; an empty day is $0.0000.
* Batch with no bucket or role → {{BatchInfraMissing}} _"BEDROCK_BATCH_S3_BUCKET and BEDROCK_BATCH_ROLE_ARN must both be set…"_
* _FAIL:_ 33 scripts still call Bedrock without the shared cache (finding 1).

_Live checks (Haiku 4.5):_ PASS 9/9

* Estimate printed before any call: _"estimated $0.000242 for 4 live calls"_.
* First call recorded: 1 miss, 1 cache file with the token usage.
* _Unchanged re-run makes no Bedrock call_, in both {{auto}} and {{replay}}: _"cache: 1 hits, 0 misses"_, same answer.
* A changed prompt, temperature or model in {{replay}} → {{CacheMissError}} _"…in replay mode -- the request changed…"_, no call.
* {{record}} always calls and rewrites the entry; {{off}} calls without reading or writing the cache; a corrupt cache file is a miss, re-fetched in {{auto}}, no crash.
* Actual cost: _$0.000037_ per call (14 in / 4 out tokens), the same from {{actual_cost_from_cache}}; about _$0.00015_ for the whole run.
* A wrapper counted every real Bedrock call: 4 in total, exactly the ones that should call.

_Findings:_

# *33 evaluation scripts still call Bedrock without the shared cache (medium, AC2).* Includes the labellers and calibrators: {{teacher_eval/judge.py}}, {{teacher_eval/online7507/label_c2..c5.py}}, {{label_pools.py}}, {{relabel_check.py}}, {{validate_label_fix.py}}, {{grading_baseline/grader.py}}, {{guardrail_curriculum/calib_grounding.py}}. {{teacher_eval/online7507/bedrock_cache.py}} is still a separate cache. Some (latency, guardrail probes, embeddings) may be fine to leave out; the migration list the docstring cites ({{results/7525-build.md}}) isn't in the repo.
# *Batch jobs can't run: no S3 bucket or role exists (medium, AC4).* {{bedrock_batch.py}} refuses clearly, as designed, and no script submits a job, so AC4 is unproven. A read-only check of the dev account (us-west-2, 1 Oct, nothing created) found: the only bucket is {{…-dev-ai-export}}, whose permissions cover {{ai-export/}} only; the only roles Bedrock can assume are the {{bedrock-cw-logging}} ones, with no S3 access; Haiku 4.5 supports batch (minimum 100 records per job) but _Sonnet 5 shows no batch quotas_, although the ticket wants Sonnet for bulk labelling. Needs a role and bucket prefix from infra. Also unproven until a real job: whether batch output (Bedrock's native body) can be read back by a harness that calls {{converse}}.
# *Batch spend would be priced at full rate (low).* {{actual_cost_from_cache()}} doesn't pass {{batch=True}} ({{cost_meter.py:123}}), so batch entries count double. They carry {{batch_record_id}}, so they can be told apart.
# *Unpriced models count as $0 (low).** {{actual_cost_from_cache()}} skips models with no price row ({{cost_meter.py:111}}), e.g. the GPT judge in {{teacher_eval/judge.py}}. The product's {{config.py}} uses the dearest price ({{FALLBACK_PRICE}}) for this.

_Not covered yet:_ a real evaluation script run twice unchanged (T11, costs real money, needs an agreed estimate); Sonnet labelling with an Opus spot-check (T13); a batch job end to end (T14, blocked on the role and bucket prefix); the measured turn still using the production model (T16).

_Observations (not failures):_

* Calls made in {{off}} mode don't appear in the cache report (_"0 hits, 0 misses"_).
* {{actual_cost_from_cache()}} totals the whole cache folder, not one run, so each harness works out its own run's cost.
* The ledger only holds runs whose script calls {{Ledger().record()}} (32 do); nothing enforces the $10 / $30 daily gate.
* Each harness folder has its own {{.cache}}, so another worktree or checkout pays again for the same requests.
* Opus prices are estimated (list × 1.1), but totals don't say so.

Details in the attached [^ONLINE-7525-test-results.docx]  (no screenshots: the evidence is the script's terminal output).

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-S: Scout cost and speed — dollar cap, cache the conversation, measure real turns, scope the guardrail
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Cost and performance

*Objective:* Lower Scout's real cost per teacher turn and speed up replies, with before-and-after figures.

*Problem:* About 12.3k tokens are processed in a typical turn, and roughly 60% of its cost is cached prompt reads. The daily cap counts only uncached tokens, so it barely limits spend. Prompt caching stops after the system prompt and tools, so each tool step re-bills the conversation history at full price. The guardrail checks the whole history on every model call.

*Expected behaviour:* Teachers get the same answers, faster and at lower cost. The daily cap limits real spend.

*Scope:*

# Measure deployed turns first: per-stage timings, cold-start rate, cache hit rate and cost per turn, from CloudWatch.
# One usage record per turn that includes cached tokens. Express the daily cap in dollars, as a code default.
# Extend prompt caching to the conversation history.
# Read the guardrail's actual cost. If it is material, check only the new user message and the model's output, behind a declared gate that keeps block/allow parity on the guardrail test cases.
# Remove dead weight: the unused {{content_cache}} table, commented-out Terraform modules, {{infra/caylent/}}, and the hard-coded user in the local dev server.

*Out of scope:* Changing Scout's models or features; the evaluation-run cache (separate ticket).

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Before and after figures for cost per turn and p50/p95 latency, on the same turn set.
# The cap is in dollars and is tested.
# Guardrail parity holds on the test cases.
# No chat-quality regression on the verify suite.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-P: Page switches stop re-paying Scout's cached prompt
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Cost and performance (follow-up to ONLINE-7526)

*Objective:* Lower Scout's cost when a teacher moves between pages, with no change to what Scout can do on each page.

*Problem:* The list of actions available on the current page sits inside a tool definition. Tool definitions are part of the cached prompt prefix, so every page switch rewrites about 9,000 cached tokens. After ONLINE-7526, this is Scout's largest remaining cost: writing the cache is about 63% of spend.

*Expected behaviour:* Teachers see no change. Scout picks the same actions on each page, and a page switch no longer invalidates the cached tools and instructions.

*Scope:*

* Move the page's action list from the tool definition into the page context message, keeping the tool definitions stable across pages.
* Keep the executor's permission checks as the authority on what can run (unchanged).

*Out of scope:* Adding or removing page actions; the daily cap and history caching (done in ONLINE-7526).

*Acceptance criteria (locked before running, arm against control on the same turn set):*

# Cost per turn on turns that follow a page switch falls by at least 20%.
# Action choice accuracy on a fixed set of page-action requests is no worse than the control.
# No action runs that the page does not offer (0 cases).
# Scout's verify suite and rag checks stay green.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-G: Scout's guardrail runs on the tier Terraform declares, and still catches every harmful request

* Apply to DEV only, with a targeted plan that touches guardrail resources alone.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-SS: Suggest standards for a teacher's own questions, in one step, from the question list
column5:
*Type / Priority tier:* Story · Teacher productivity (replaces SCOUT-07's per-question standards suggestions)

*Objective:* When a teacher explicitly asks for it, Scout suggests likely standards for the teacher's own questions or a topic. The teacher reviews and accepts the suggestions quickly, without any interruption to how they build the assignment.

*Principles (Salman, 2026-09-27):*

* *Never assume what the teacher hasn't explicitly asked for.* An information request ("which articles cover standard X", "what standards does this week cover") is answered only from SWO data. A suggestion request ("suggest standards that could cover this topic", or the Suggest standards button) may return AI suggestions.
* *Studies Weekly content is the source of truth.* Suggested codes come only from the SWO standards catalogue for the teacher's state. Related content comes only from our publications. Scout never states which standards Studies Weekly content covers from its own judgement.
* *Teacher-written questions outside our publications:* suggestions are allowed if the question is educational and passes the guardrails. Non-educational or personal requests are declined.
* *Never blocks the regular flow.* No dialog on save and no required step.
* *Clearly labelled:* "Suggested by AI. It can make mistakes, so please review before accepting."
* *Behind the AI feature flag.* Users without it see no change and make no request.

*Expected behaviour:*

* *Question list:* on the customized-content create/edit page, where all questions are listed, a quiet "Suggest standards" action appears when one or more questions have no standard. One click sends *one request* for all of those questions, not one per question.
* *Suggestions:* each question's standards area shows its suggested standards with a short reason. The teacher can accept or dismiss each one, or accept all. An accepted standard is added exactly like one picked by hand. Nothing is added without a click.
* *In Scout chat:* when a teacher explicitly asks for standards suggestions for a topic or question, Scout returns labelled suggestions from the SWO catalogue. It never presents them as Studies Weekly alignments.

*Scope:*

* Reuse the question-level suggestion engine kept from ONLINE-7513 (rag), extended to take many questions in one call.
* Cost: one model call per click, with a cap on questions per call and the estimate recorded per call.

*Out of scope:* suggestions for Studies Weekly content; any content-team review pipeline; save-time pop-ups.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# One request per click, whatever the number of questions (up to the cap).
# No suggestion is written without the teacher accepting it. Once accepted, a standard is indistinguishable from a hand-picked one.
# The disclaimer is shown with every suggestion set, both on the page and in chat.
# Users without the AI flag see no change on the page, and no request is made.
# Suggested codes always exist in the SWO standards catalogue for the teacher's state.
# Information requests about Studies Weekly content never return AI suggestions. This is covered by a test set of lookup requests: 0 suggestions on those.
# Non-educational or personal requests are declined, and every request passes the guardrails.
# A quality gate is declared before release: precision on a labelled set of teacher questions, with the bar set before the run, and a cost estimate.
# Backend tests: happy path, 422, and 403 for the wrong role and for another district or school.

Nothing is saved, but the tool tells the model "never that you added or attached them" (rag 64099335), and the ticket's rule is that nothing is added without a click. It also says "card above" although the card is below.

h1. _Literal underscores in the card (low)._

h1. _Standard lookup contradicts the week (medium, likely the lookup rather than this ticket):_

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT: Stable student aliases across tabs and conversations
column5:
*Objective:* Keep student references in Scout stable and non-identifying, so a reopened conversation never points at the wrong child.

*Problem:* Student names never leave the browser. Scout sees per-tab counters ("Student 30"), which reset in every tab. In a reopened conversation, "Student 30" from earlier turns can now refer to a different child, and Scout could act on the wrong student.

*Expected behaviour:*

* Each student gets a short code derived from their permanent id, e.g. "Student K7QM4R".
* The code is the same for that teacher across tabs and sessions.
* The code can't be reversed to an id and can't be linked across teachers.
* The browser maps codes back to names. Names still never leave the browser.

*Design* (approved by Salman, 2026-09-28; handoff {{results/stable-student-alias-design.md}}):

* *Keys:* per-teacher key K_t = HMAC-SHA256(APP_KEY, "scout-student-alias:v1:" + teacher_id). This uses the existing APP_KEY, so no new env var is needed.
* *Endpoint:* a teacher-only {{GET ai/alias-key}} returns K_t. The tab keeps it in memory only; it is never sent to rag.
* *Code format:* 6 characters from consonants and the digits 2–9, starting with a letter. Two students with the same code both get an 8-character code.
* *Browser library:* {{@noble/hashes}} is added to frontend-v3 for synchronous HMAC.
* *Shared pattern:* rag and the browser share one alias pattern. The name scrub ({{name_scrub.py}}) and every "Student \d+" regex are updated.
* *Existing conversations:* left as is (Salman).
* *Key rotation:* rotating APP_KEY at go-live changes every code. Accepted.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# The same student gets the same code in two tabs, and again after a reload, for the same teacher.
# Two teachers get different codes for the same student.
# The key never appears in any request to rag, in Mongo, in logs or in telemetry.
# No real name reaches rag, Mongo or logs; the name-scrub checks pass with the new pattern.
# A mistyped or unknown code resolves to no student and never to a different child.
# Everything is behind the AI flag, with zero change for non-AI users.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT: @-mention students in the Scout message box
column5:
*Objective:* Let a teacher pick a student precisely in Scout's message box by typing @, so Scout always knows which student is meant and no student name ever has to be guessed from free text.

*Problem:* Today Scout codes student names it recognises in typed text before anything leaves the browser. Exact names work, but a typo ("Micheal"), a nickname ("Mike"), or two students with the same name can't be matched reliably, and a capitalised word that is also a student's first name ("Will you make a quiz?") can be mistaken for a student.

*Expected behaviour:*

* Typing *@* in Scout's message box opens a list of the teacher's students: the open class first, then other classes, with each student's class shown and dropped students labelled "Dropped".
* Typing after @ filters the list. Arrow keys, Enter and Esc work; mouse and touch work.
* Choosing a student inserts a chip showing the student's name. Backspace next to a chip removes the whole chip.
* The sent message carries the student's code, never the name. The model never sees a name.
* The chip shows the same way in the sent message bubble, when the message is edited, in Copy (which copies the name), and when the conversation is reopened.
* Automatic coding of typed names stays as the safety net for text typed or pasted without @.
* The Meet Scout tour and the message box placeholder tell teachers "Type @ to pick a student".

*Notes:*

* Student list comes from the alias roster Scout already loads (current and dropped students); no new endpoint.
* New component only, using {{--swo-color-*}} tokens; the approved design is otherwise unchanged.
* Everything behind the AI flag; zero change for non-AI users.

*Acceptance criteria:*

# @ opens the list; typing filters it; choosing inserts a chip with the student's name.
# Backspace removes a whole chip.
# The request to rag carries the student's code for every chip; no chip name appears in the request.
# Two students with the same name are distinguishable in the list by class.
# Chips survive edit, Copy (as names) and reopening the conversation.
# Typing without @ behaves as today.
# Keyboard-only use works; the list is announced to screen readers.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT: generate several questions at once for Customized Content
column5:
h2. Why

The AI Question Generator in Customized Content makes one question per run. Teachers who want a set have to repeat the whole flow for each question. The service can already write a checked set of up to 5 questions in one run, but the browser only ever asks it for 1.

h2. Flow

* *Entry:* the "Save time with the AI Question Generator!" box on the Customized Content create and edit forms opens Scout with a short form. The per-type AI option under *+Add › Question* stays as it is now: one question of the type the teacher picked.
* *Form fields:*
** *Publication:* optional, as today.
** *Grade:* required, because it sets how hard the questions are.
** *How many questions:* 1 to 5, default 3.
** *Question types:* one or more types. If the teacher picks one type, every question uses it. If they pick several, the types are spread across the set.
** *What should the questions be about?:* optional, as today.
* *Results:* Scout shows the set as one card. Every question is ticked. The teacher can untick any question, or refine the set in chat.
* *Apply:* "Add N questions" appends the ticked questions to the Customized Content in order. Each one is added the same way a single generated question is added today. The rest of the flow (students, instructions, due date, save) does not change.
* *Limit:* 5 per run, because that is the service's checked-set size. For more, the teacher runs it again.

h2. Scope

* Behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher Customized Content only.
* Built on its own branch and not merged into the combined Scout branch until Salman has tested it.

h2. Acceptance criteria

* 1, 3 and 5 questions generate, show and add correctly. The added blocks match the cards and appear in order.
* A single type gives that type for every question. Several types are each used.
* Unticked questions are not added.
* Grade is required. Publication and topic stay optional.
* Single-question generation from *+Add › Question* is unchanged.
* Reopening the conversation shows the same set.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-PR: Production readiness fixes from the October 2 audit
column5:
Code fixes found by a production-readiness review of Scout (safety, privacy, failure behaviour). They are all needed before go-live. Go-live steps that need prod access are tracked separately in ONLINE-7489, 7491, 7494 and 7500.

*Security*

* The "forget" memory request accepts only a valid memory id.
* The API checks a user's sign-in against the right environment's site only.
* Bulk coin awards check the teacher's class and have a limit.
* Undo checks that the teacher can still change that class.
* Scout saves or forgets a memory only when the teacher asked for it.
* Search records can be read only by their owner.
* Repeated failed sign-ins don't slow Scout down for other teachers.

*Privacy*

* Logs don't store conversation text or full replies.
* Student emails and usernames don't leave the app for Scout.
* Removing a user also removes their Scout conversations.
* Scout's screens are hidden from analytics recordings.

*Reliability*

* An approved action never runs twice when a teacher retries.
* Scout fails fast when its database is slow, instead of piling up requests.
* A missing Scout address in settings is reported clearly.
* Long turns count toward the daily limit.
* Alerts fire when a usage limit isn't being applied.

*Non-AI users*

* Scout's code doesn't load or run for teachers without Scout.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-Z: Scout's own dropdowns and dialogs always stay above the Scout window
column5:
*Problem:* A dropdown opened inside Scout (e.g. Question types in the question form) can open behind the Scout window. Vuetify opens the menu on mousedown and the field takes focus afterwards. The window re-raises itself on focus ({{AiAssistantDialog.vue}}, {{@focusin}}/{{@pointerdown.capture}} → {{raiseLayer}}), so it jumps above its own open menu. It returns whenever a component's event order changes.

*Fix:* Raising Scout's window or one of its panels also raises every Scout-owned overlay still open ({{ai-overlay}}), right above it, in the same order ({{ai/zIndex.ts}}). Page popups keep "last opened on top" (R114).

*Acceptance criteria:*

# Every dropdown, dialog and toast opened from Scout shows in front of the Scout window, whatever the click or focus order.
# A page modal opened over Scout is still in front; clicking back into Scout brings Scout and its open menus to the front together.
# Two tests fail on today's code and pass after the fix: the event-order test, and a real-browser test of a real dropdown inside the Scout window.
# Teachers without the AI flag see no change.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-PA: Prompt restructure: shared core, rules travel with the feature
column5:
*Goal:* in priority order, keep or improve response quality, lower cost, and keep or improve speed. Scout's chat prompt stops growing with every feature. Today every chat call carries about 17.7k identical tokens: about 8.8k of rules and 8.6k of tool descriptions for 18 tools.

*Design:* handoff {{results/prompt-architecture-review-2026-10-03.md}}, corrected by {{results/prompt-restructure-quality-audit-2026-10-03.md}}.

* A shared core of about 5.2k tokens holds every rule that must stay global (24 clusters).
* Tool descriptions say only when to use each tool.
* Tool results carry facts only, never rules.
* Page modules load deterministically.
* No {{read_guide}} tool.
* The engine prompts are left unchanged (DEV-149).
* A per-teacher cached layer holds the "About you" block.
* A test caps the core plus tools.

*Phases:*

# A sentence-level rule registry and pins: every current rule has exactly one home or a dated deletion. The recitation screen is rebuilt from the registry.
1a. Cache-point changes only, proven byte-identical.
# The restructure, merged only if the quality gate passes.

*Acceptance criteria (quality first):*

# The gate is declared before any rows: 300 frozen asks × 2 per side plus 40 threads, arm vs control at named shas.
# Task success and correct tool or action choice are no worse than control within the declared margin. Every existing quality and safety screen stays at its current bar. A pairwise judge, validated first, is used as do-no-harm.
# Cost and latency are reported only after quality passes.
# Approved spend is about $55, run across two days.

column3: [AI Project] Scout: AiScoutFeedbackReportTest fails intermittently because the AI report is read from a shared Redis cache left by earlier tests
column5:
{{Tests\Feature\AiScoutFeedbackReportTest::testAFailedTurnRowInflatesNoOtherReport}} fails at random in CI {{tests:backend}}. It failed on 4 of about 50 security MR pipelines on 2026-10-08 (!6065, !6073, !6074, !6094). Each failure has the same diff: the first read has no {{model-x}} rows, and the second read has them.

*Cause:* {{AiReportController}} caches {{/api/ai/reports}} for 60 seconds under a key built from the dates, model filter and timezone. Tests use {{CACHE_DRIVER=redis}} (phpunit.xml), so the cache is shared and is not cleared between tests. If an earlier test cached the {{timezone=UTC}} report less than 60 seconds before, the test's first read ({{UTC}}) returns that stale, empty report. Its second read ({{Etc/UTC}}, a fresh key) sees the real rows, so the two reads differ. Whether it fails depends on test order and timing, which is why branches that add tests trip it more often.

*Fix:* make this test class use the per-process {{array}} cache store, so every test starts with an empty cache. This is a test-only change; no app code changes.

*Acceptance:* the test passes regardless of which tests ran before it, and the CI {{tests:backend}} job is green on the fix MR.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-RC: Report card comments drafted from the teacher's own gradebook
column5:
*Why:* Writing report card comments is one of the most time-consuming teacher tasks. Generic AI tools (for example MagicSchool's Report Card Comments) need the teacher to type in each student's strengths. Scout already has the student's real work in SWO, so its comments can be grounded in evidence.

*Flow*

* The teacher asks, for example: "Write report card comments for my class for this quarter", "Comments for @Sam and @Ava", or uses a hint on the gradebook or student pages.
* Scout asks only for what's missing: which students, the date range (default: this quarter), the length (short or a paragraph), and the tone.
* For each student, the draft names one or two strengths and one growth area. Each one is tied to evidence: an assignment, a skill or standard, or a trend, such as scores rising across three weeks.
* The drafts appear as one card: one comment per student, each with Copy, and a Copy all.
* The teacher can refine the comments in chat, for example "shorter" or "warmer for Sam".

*Rules*

* Names show on screen. Only codes reach the model, as in Scout today.
* A student with too little work in the range gets "Not enough work this quarter" instead of a made-up comment.
* No grades or comments are written back to SWO or any SIS. These are drafts to copy.
* Comments are suitable for the student's grade (K–8) and free of diagnostic or medical language.
* Remembered and reopened conversations show the same comments.

*Reuse:* this builds on the student-profile and family-draft work (ONLINE-7516) and the student performance data (ONLINE-7510). There are no new tables, and no new endpoint if the existing data covers it.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# One student and a whole class (25 or more) both draft correctly, with evidence that matches the gradebook.
# A student with no work in the range is labelled, not invented.
# No name appears in the request to Scout Core.
# Copy and Copy all work. Reopening the conversation shows the same drafts.
# A declared quality gate is set before any rows are reviewed. It checks that each piece of evidence matches the student's data, and that no comment is generic.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-RB: Rubric for a written question or assignment
column5:
*Why:* Teachers who grade written answers need a rubric, both to score consistently and to share expectations with students. Generic tools (for example MagicSchool's Rubric Generator) start from a typed topic. Scout can start from the actual question, the article it is about, and its answer key.

*Flow*

* The teacher can ask "Make a rubric for this question" on a written question, in Grade Now or in Customized Content.
* They can also ask "Make a rubric for this assignment" on an assignment.
* Or they can ask from chat with a topic and grade.
* Scout asks only for what's missing: the grade (from the class when known), the number of levels (default 4) and the point scale.
* The rubric appears as a card:
** criteria as rows, levels as columns, with a short, observable description in each cell;
** Copy;
** refining it in chat ("add a criterion for evidence from the text").

*Rules*

* Criteria come from the question, the article and the answer key. Scout never invents facts about Studies Weekly content.
* Language suits the grade (K–8).
* The rubric is a draft to copy. In this ticket it does not change scores, and Grade Now does not use it yet. Using it in Grade Now's review is a possible follow-up, once teachers have tried it.
* Remembered and reopened conversations show the same rubric.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change. There are no new tables.

*Acceptance criteria*

# A rubric is drafted from a Grade Now question, from a Customized Content written question, and from a typed topic.
# The criteria match the question asked, and the cells describe observable work.
# The levels and the scale follow the teacher's choice.
# Copy pastes cleanly into Google Docs and Word as a table.
# Reopening the conversation shows the same rubric.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-FB: Grade Now review drafts feedback for the student
column5:
*Why:* Grade Now's review tells the teacher which answers need a closer look. Writing a comment to each student is still manual. MagicSchool's Writing Feedback produces student-facing feedback, but only from writing pasted in by hand. Scout already has the question, its answer key and the student's answer.

*Flow*

* On a reviewed answer in Grade Now, the teacher can ask Scout to "Draft feedback for this student" or "Draft feedback for all reviewed answers".
* Scout drafts, for each answer:
** one strength, quoting the student's own words;
** one thing to fix, and why;
** one next step.
* The draft is written to the student, in language that suits their grade (K–8), in about 40–80 words.
* The card shows a Copy button for each draft. If the comment box is on screen, it also shows "Put in comment box", which fills the box but does not save.
* The teacher edits the comment and saves it as they do today.

*Rules*

* Every quote is the student's real text. Nothing is claimed that isn't in the answer.
* No score is suggested or changed.
* Only codes reach the model.
* Nothing is saved without the teacher pressing Save.
* Reopened conversations show the same drafts.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT and FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTED_GRADING. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# Drafts are produced for one answer and for every reviewed answer.
# The quotes match the student's answers exactly.
# "Put in comment box" fills the box without saving it.
# Reopening the conversation shows the same drafts.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-TR: Translate family message drafts
column5:
*Why:* Many families don't read English. Scout already drafts family messages (ONLINE-7516). Teachers then paste them into a separate translator, and the formatting is lost.

*Flow*

* The family draft card gets a "Translate" action with a short language list (Spanish first, then the most common languages in our districts) and an "Other language" box.
* Scout returns the translated draft beside the English one, each with its own Copy button. The teacher can also ask in chat, for example "translate that into Vietnamese".

*Rules*

* Names, dates, class names and links are kept exactly as they are.
* The tone and meaning match the English draft. Nothing is added.
* The card notes that the text was machine-translated and should be checked before sending.
* Only codes reach the model.
* Reopened conversations show both versions.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change. There are no new tables.

*Acceptance criteria*

# Spanish and one other language translate, with names, dates and links unchanged.
# Copy gives the translated text.
# Reopening the conversation shows both versions.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-DOK: Depth-of-knowledge mix in generated question sets
column5:
*Why:* Teachers often want a set that moves beyond recall. MagicSchool has a separate DOK Questions tool. We can add the option to the question-set form we already have (ONLINE-7567).

*Flow*

* The multi-question form gets an optional "Depth of knowledge" choice:
** Any (default, the same as today);
** Mostly recall (DOK 1);
** Mixed (DOK 1–3);
** Mostly reasoning (DOK 2–3).
* Each generated question shows a small DOK label on the card.
* The teacher can ask in chat to "make question 3 harder" or "add a DOK 3 question".

*Rules*

* The questions stay grounded in the article. DOK 3 questions ask for reasoning about the article's content, never for facts that aren't in it.
* The DOK label is Scout's estimate and is shown as such.
* Single-question generation is unchanged.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher Customized Content only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# "Any" gives the same behaviour as today.
# "Mixed" on a 5-question set includes at least one DOK 1 and at least one DOK 2–3 question.
# The labels show on the card and are not added to the saved question text.
# A declared check is set before running. A Sonnet label on 40 or more generated questions agrees with the requested level at least 80% of the time.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-EX: Exemplar and non-exemplar answers for a written question
column5:
*Why:* Showing students a strong and a weak answer is a common way to teach what good work looks like. MagicSchool has a separate Exemplar & Non-Exemplar tool. Scout can write them from the actual question, its article and its answer key. If a rubric exists (ONLINE-7754), Scout matches the samples to it.

*Flow*

* On a written question, in Customized Content, in Grade Now or in chat, the teacher can ask Scout to "Show a strong and a weak answer".
* Scout drafts:
** one exemplar;
** one non-exemplar with a common mistake;
** a short note for each, saying why it is strong or weak (for example, which rubric criterion it meets or misses).
* The card shows Copy for each sample and Copy all.

*Rules*

* The samples use only facts from the article and its answer key.
* The samples are clearly labelled as made-up. They are never presented as a real student's work, and never use a real student's answer.
* Language suits the grade (K–8).
* Reopened conversations show the same samples.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# Samples are produced from a Customized Content question, a Grade Now question and a typed question.
# Both samples match the article's facts.
# When a rubric is present in the conversation, the notes refer to its criteria.
# Reopening the conversation shows the same samples.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-SL: Scout drafts a lesson walkthrough from the Studies Weekly article
column5:
*Why:* Teachers build slides for almost every lesson. MagicSchool's newest tool, the Presentation Generator, makes decks from a topic or pasted text. SWO already has lesson walkthroughs: slide decks the teacher presents and students view. Scout can draft a walkthrough from the actual Studies Weekly article, with its images, vocabulary and questions, and the teacher presents it in the walkthrough player they already use.

This is one ticket. Everything is done inside it.

*Flow*

* The teacher can start from an article or week ("Make a walkthrough for this lesson"), from Teacher Resources, or from chat with an article named.
* Scout asks only for what's missing:
** the number of slides;
** what to include: a hook, key ideas, vocabulary, a check-for-understanding question, a discussion prompt or an exit ticket;
** teacher notes on or off.
* The grade comes from the class.
* Scout drafts walkthrough slides:
** a title and short, grade-appropriate text on each slide;
** the article's own images;
** vocabulary from the article;
** questions grounded in the text;
** teacher notes on teacher-only slides or in the teacher guide.
* The teacher previews and presents the deck in the existing walkthrough player. They can edit the text, reorder or delete slides, and refine through chat ("add a slide on the rookery", "simpler words").
* Where possible, Scout can also add slides to the article's existing Studies Weekly walkthrough, such as a check-for-understanding slide after slide 3, without changing the original.
* The teacher's walkthrough is saved and assigned through Customized Content, if its walkthrough block can hold teacher slides. That is settled in the design note.

*Rules*

* Content comes from the article and our publication data only. Scout never adds facts that aren't in the article. Any extension is labelled as Scout's suggestion.
* Images are used only from our own publication assets, never generated.
* Language suits the grade (K–8).
* Existing walkthroughs look and behave exactly as today. Any player change only adds to what it can do.
* Reopened conversations show the same deck.

*Open design questions (in the design note, for Salman):*

* Where a teacher's walkthrough is saved.
* Whether .pptx or Google Slides export is wanted.
* Image use outside SWO.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# A walkthrough is drafted from an article, from a week and from chat.
# Every fact on a slide traces to the article. This is a declared check, set before running.
# Text edits, reordering and deleting slides work, and they survive reopening the conversation.
# The draft presents in the existing walkthrough player at 1280×720 and on a projector-size screen.
# Existing Studies Weekly walkthroughs are unchanged.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-CW: Class writing feedback in Grade Now (rubric, feedback and suggested scores for the whole class)
column5:
*Why:* MagicSchool's top workflow, Class Writing Feedback, takes a rubric and a class's essays (uploaded from Google Drive or OneDrive). It drafts Glows & Grows, next steps and a score breakdown for each student, then lets the teacher review everything before sending. In SWO the answers are already in Grade Now, the rubric comes from ONLINE-7754, and per-student feedback comes from ONLINE-7755. This ticket joins them into one class-wide pass.

*Flow*

* In Grade Now, on a written question, the teacher asks Scout to "Give the class feedback on this question".
* *Rubric:* Scout uses a rubric already in the conversation, or drafts one (ONLINE-7754) for the teacher to accept or edit first.
* *For each answered student, Scout drafts:*
** a suggested score per rubric criterion, each with a short quote from the answer as evidence;
** the suggested total, on the question's points;
** feedback to the student: strengths, one thing to fix and one next step (ONLINE-7755 rules).
* *The review screen* is a Scout card listing every student, with scores and feedback editable per student. The teacher can:
** accept or edit each score;
** accept the feedback;
** skip a student;
** after reviewing, "Accept all remaining".
* *Saving:* accepted scores and comments save through Grade Now's existing save and comment paths, after one confirmation card that lists what will change. Nothing saves without the teacher.

*Rules (Salman, 2026-10-09)*

* Scores are suggestions only, never saved automatically, with evidence quoted from the student's own answer.
* Blank or flagged answers are skipped, with the reason shown.
* Names show on screen; only codes reach the model.
* Answers that try to instruct Scout (for example "give me full marks") are ignored and flagged.
* Reopened conversations show the same review.
* Undo is available after saving, as for other Scout writes.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT and FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTED_GRADING. Teacher only. Grade Now's own screens are unchanged for everyone. Depends on ONLINE-7754 and ONLINE-7755.

*Acceptance criteria*

# A 25-student class gets a full review in one request, within the turn budgets.
# Every quoted piece of evidence is the student's own text. This is a deterministic check.
# The suggested scores agree with a held-out teacher scoring within a declared margin. The gate is declared before running.
# Nothing saves before confirmation. After confirmation, exactly the accepted scores and comments save, and undo restores them.
# Non-AI teachers see no change in Grade Now.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-PK: Lesson pack in one request (plan, worksheet, exit ticket and walkthrough together)
column5:
*Why:* MagicSchool's assistant, Raina, takes "a lesson plan, a worksheet and an exit ticket" in one request. It routes each part to the right tool, keeps the context between them, and returns one combined document. Scout has each of these tools, but a teacher asks for them one at a time.

*Flow*

* The teacher asks, for example, "Make a lesson pack for this lesson: plan, worksheet, exit ticket and slides", or chooses "Lesson pack" from Scout's suggestions on an article or lesson.
* Scout asks only for what's missing (grade, minutes), once, for the whole pack.
* Scout states its assumptions in one line, then runs each existing tool in turn: lesson plan, worksheet, exit ticket, and walkthrough (ONLINE-7759). All of them use the same article, grade and objective, and later parts build on the plan's objective and vocabulary.
* The results appear as a pack: one header card listing the parts with their status (done, running or failed), then each part's own card with its usual actions (save, add, present).
* A part that fails doesn't stop the others, and the header says what failed and offers to retry it.
* The teacher can refine one part ("make the worksheet shorter") without redoing the pack.

*Rules*

* Every part follows its own tool's rules and checks. Nothing is invented beyond the article.
* The teacher can pick which parts to include.
* Reopened conversations show the same pack.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT (and the lesson-plans flag for the plan part). Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change. There are no new tables.

*Acceptance criteria*

# A four-part pack completes in one request within the turn budgets, or the plan states clearly how the request is split.
# All parts share the grade and objective, and the worksheet and exit ticket use the plan's vocabulary.
# One failed part leaves the others intact, with a retry offered.
# Refining one part changes only that part.
# Reopening the conversation shows the same pack.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-SC: Saved Scout shortcuts with fixed settings
column5:
*Why:* MagicSchool lets a teacher customise any tool. Fields can be hidden and locked (for example, grade fixed at 4), and hidden instructions can be added, so a request the teacher repeats is one click. Scout teachers repeat requests too ("exit ticket, 5 questions, grade 4, include vocabulary"), and have to retype them every time.

*Flow*

* After any Scout result, the teacher can choose "Save as shortcut". Scout proposes:
** a name;
** the request;
** its fixed settings (grade, length, number of questions, tone, parts to include);
** optional extra instructions.
* The teacher edits and saves.
* Shortcuts appear in Scout as one-click chips under "My shortcuts", and in "What Scout can do". Running one fills in the current page's article or class and runs it straight away, or asks only for what the shortcut leaves open.
* The teacher can rename, edit or delete a shortcut.

*Rules*

* Shortcuts are private to the teacher. There is no sharing in this ticket.
* A shortcut can't bypass any Scout rule or approval, and its extra instructions are treated as the teacher's request, not as system rules.
* A maximum of 20 shortcuts per teacher.

*Storage:* a new {{ai_scout_shortcuts}} table (user, name, request, settings JSON), with endpoints that have auth, a policy and tests per AGENTS.md. Alternatively, reuse the Scout memories store if it fits; the design note decides.

*Scope:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# Save, run, edit and delete work, and a shortcut survives reload and new conversations.
# Fixed settings are applied without asking. Open settings are asked once.
# Another teacher can't read or run a teacher's shortcuts (403 test).
# Extra instructions can't turn off approvals or grounding. This is a declared check.

column3: [AI Project] SCOUT-QT: AI question generator writes Drawing and Hot Text questions
column5:
*Why:* Scout's question generator writes 9 of the editor's 13 question types. Drawing, Hot Text, Labeling and Hot Spot were left out early on. An experiment on 2026-10-09 ({{results/QUESTION-TYPES-EXPERIMENT-2026-10-09.md}}) found:

* Drawing is ready: 7 of 8 samples were usable, with a valid block shape on 8 of 8.
* Hot Text needs one fix: 6 of 8 were usable, and the answer key graded correctly on 8 of 8.
* Labeling and Hot Spot need positions on a picture that nothing supplies. They are parked.

*Scope (Salman, 2026-10-09)*

* *Drawing:* a question grounded in the article, with a model-answer checklist for the teacher, since drawing is graded by hand. It can optionally use the article's own picture as the background. No generated images.
* *Hot Text:* the model chooses the article sentences and the correct phrases. Code builds the passage from the article's exact sentences, so it always quotes the article word for word. The answer key is checked in code.
* Both are written only when the teacher names the type, in the multi-question form, the per-type AI option under +Add › Question, or chat. They are not added to the default mix.
* Question sets, refine, replay and adding to Customized Content work as they do for the other types.

*Not in scope:* Labeling and Hot Spot. They are parked until a small measurement of pin placement on real article diagrams (about $0.50).

*Scope rules:* behind FEATURE_FRONTEND_AI_ASSISTANT. Teacher only. Non-AI users see no change.

*Acceptance criteria*

# Every generated Drawing and Hot Text block passes the editor's own shape, and saves and renders like a hand-made one.
# Every Hot Text passage is an exact excerpt of the article, and its answer key grades correctly. Both are deterministic checks.
# Every Drawing question has a model-answer checklist and doesn't give the answer away.
# A declared gate on fresh articles, run once.

column3: [AI Project] Yearly planning calendar: place a publication's weeks on real dates, import the school calendar, and let Scout's pacing use it
column5:
Teachers have no way to lay a publication's weeks onto their school year. Scout's pacing guesses the year from the class's start and end dates, which are still the create-form defaults for 57,175 of 57,503 dated classes on the dev snapshot. This adds a planning calendar per class and publication, and pacing reads it. Idea from the sales pilot "Studies Weekly Intelligence Pilot" (Recommendation 1).

*Decisions (Salman, 2026-10-10)*

* One calendar per class and publication.
* Dates a teacher tells Scout are saved to the calendar with approval; the conversation-only override (ruling 2026-09-28) is removed.
* Entry point: a "Plan the year" button on the class's publication page. No change to the menu, hamburger or search.
* Own feature flag {{FEATURE_PLANNING_CALENDAR}} (a FeatureFlag constant, no environment variable).
* Tables {{classroom_calendars}}, {{classroom_calendar_days}}, {{classroom_calendar_weeks}}.
* Import from iCal and CSV in this ticket; PDF and image import later.

*Acceptance criteria*

# From the class's publication page, "Plan the year" opens the class's calendar for that publication, seeded with the class's dates (or August to May when those are the defaults).
# Weeks not placed show as suggested, spread evenly over the school days. A week can be dragged onto a date or given a date from its menu; the weeks after it move along, skipping no-school days, except weeks placed by hand.
# Clicking a date adds an event or marks a day or range as no school. Events can be edited and deleted.
# An .ics or .csv school calendar can be imported; the teacher sees a preview and confirms before anything saves.
# "My calendars" lists the class's calendars; each reopens as saved and prints (year view on one page, month views one per page).
# With a saved calendar, "Where is my class", "Plan my next weeks", the replan and the daily briefing use it and say so; without one, they behave as today.
# Scout schedules from plain requests ("Start Week 5 on November 3", "We're off Nov 24 to 28", "I teach Monday, Wednesday and Friday") through an approval card listing every change, then a receipt with Undo.
# Dates the teacher tells Scout are saved to the calendar with approval; the conversation-only override is removed.
# Only the class's teachers (and a masquerading admin) can read or change it; students, other teachers and other districts are refused. Flag off: no button, no page, no Scout ability.
# Flag-off teachers see no change.

*Tests:* backend feature tests per route (happy path, 422, 403 for the wrong role and another district, flag off); pacing unit tests for the saved calendar; import parser tests; Scout action approval, receipt and Undo; frontend date pins.

*Not included:* district or school calendars that teachers inherit, and PDF or image import (later ticket); unit-level features (teachers plan by week; "Schedule Unit 3 in November" places that unit's weeks); minutes per lesson; students and families; the legacy app.

column5:
The rag repo grew through many AI-assisted changes and has to stand up to an outside senior review. A read-only review (2026-10-10) compared it with the Caylent baseline and best practice and found 17 issues. This ticket works through them phase by phase, pinning behaviour before any move. Rulings are needed before phases 7 and 8.

*Main findings*

* No CI and no single test entry point: 133 check scripts, which pytest does not collect; one runner covers 90 of them and the README 44.
* Two generations in one package: a legacy agent kept for stored checkpoints, two endpoints registered twice, two Lambda functions and two Dockerfiles built from one source.
* About 1,170 lines of dead code in 6 modules with no importer.
* Docs point outside the repo (173 section references to a swo-3.0 doc); the lambda README is out of date; most experiment folders have no README.
* Two settings systems, two price tables, five syllable counters, hard-coded account-bound ARNs.
* 30 functions over 100 lines; 23 silent exception handlers.

*Phases (estimated hours at AI speed)*

||Phase||Scope||Hours||
|0|Baseline run, route and prompt snapshots, pytest wrapper, CI with no deploy stage|4|
|1|Delete the dead code (each deletion approved) and unused dependencies|3|
|2|Repo tidy for a reader: root clutter, READMEs, section references, experiments index|8|
|3|One settings module and one price table|5|
|4|Shared test harness|6|
|5|Logging and silent handlers|5|
|6|Dedupe helpers, prompt index|6|

column3: [AI Project] Scout exports: download any Scout answer as CSV (figures) or PDF (text), on request, for teachers and admins
column5:
h2. Goal

When a teacher or admin asks for it, Scout offers a download of what it just gave them:

* *CSV* (opens in Excel) for numbers and tables, such as class results, standards, pacing and Insights figures.
* *PDF* for text, such as lesson plans, family drafts, meeting summaries and rubrics.

Downloads are never shown by default, only when asked. This is one shared Scout feature, not something built page by page.

h2. How it works

* *Numbers come from data, not from Scout's wording.* A CSV is built on the server from the same data the Scout tool read. Scout only offers the download, so the file can never hold a number Scout made up or copied wrong.
* *PDF from text.* A PDF is made from content the teacher reviews before using: a lesson plan, a draft, a summary.
* *One export door.* Each Scout tool that returns a table registers that data as downloadable. One endpoint builds the CSV or PDF.
* *Admin exports move onto it.* The district summary and principal brief from ONLINE-7806 become the first data sources, so admin and teacher exports work the same way, not as two systems.

h2. Rules

* *Same permissions as the existing reports.* Teachers get only their own students. Admin exports never contain student names. Nothing can be exported while logged in as someone else.
* *Spreadsheet formulas.* CSV cells that start with {{=}}, {{+}}, {{-}} or {{@}} are escaped.
* *Feature flag.* Behind a flag; users with it off see no change.

h2. Out of scope

* Native .xlsx files (CSV opens in Excel).
* Charts or images.

column3: [AI Project] Level text button on articles: 1 or 2 grades down, grade rules and an assessment warning
column5:
From the Oct 15 Scout product review. Behind the Scout flag; flag-off users see no change.

h2. Scope

* *Level text button* beside the article. It opens Scout with the leveling prompt already set and asks only: 1 grade down or 2 grades down. It is a shortcut into Scout, not a separate tool.
* *Grade rules* (same rules as the question generator's text leveler):
** No button on Kindergarten and 1st grade articles.
** 2nd grade levels down to 1st only.
** Grades 3 to 8 level down 1 or 2 grades.
** Never level up.
* *Assessment warning* on every leveled text: leveling can leave out information students need for the article questions and assessments. Wording adapted from the message district admins see when they turn off an article.
* *Same limits in Scout chat*: when a teacher asks Scout in their own words to level an article, apply the same grade rules, refuse leveling up, and show the same warning.
* Leveled text is saved to Customized Content only on the teacher's request and never replaces the publication's own text.

h2. Later in this ticket

* Measured check: level a set of articles and record whether each article's comprehension and quiz questions can still be answered from the leveled text; results reviewed by the content team.

h2. Not in this ticket

* Editorially written leveled versions for every article (ONLINE-5212).
* IEP/504 students always seeing leveled text.

h2. Done when

* The button appears only on grades 2 to 8 articles with the right choices, every leveled text carries the warning, and a chat request to level up or go 3+ grades down is refused.

column3: [AI Project] Scout cost: measured cost per tool and a weekly usage cap per teacher
column5:
From the Oct 15 Scout product review and the follow-up on cost. This ticket covers how much a teacher can use Scout. Who gets Scout (district opt-in, seats, school-year licenses, pilots) moved to ONLINE-7874 on 2026-10-20.

h2. Cost

* *Measure each tool's cost* (lesson pack, slides, weekly plan, leveling, report cards, class feedback, District Insights questions) from the per-turn cost already logged.
* *Weekly usage cap per teacher*, sized to medium use so a seat stays within its yearly price. Counted in AI cost, not messages, so a lesson pack uses more than a quick question. When reached, Scout says when the allowance resets. Existing per-user rate limits stay.

h2. Related

* ONLINE-7874 (access and licensing), ONLINE-7489 (prod monitoring and cost control), ONLINE-5621 (payment for AI tools).

h2. Done when

* A teacher over the weekly cap is stopped with the reset time.
